entries.title: White Sox use patient approach, move to 4-1 on the year against AL strikeout leader Gavin Williams
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — Add the White Sox’ performance in Game 2 of the American League Division Series to their four games in the regular season against Guardians starter <b>Gavin Williams</b> and it doesn’t look too bad at first for the AL strikeout leader.</p><p>Williams has a 3.91 ERA against the Sox, who have the AL’s best scoring offense. After punching out 11 in five-plus innings Monday in Cleveland, his strikeout rate against all hitters this year is a whopping 36.4%.</p><p>But he failed to earn the “W” in any of his starts against the Sox and has walked their hitters 10.3% of the time. The Guardians won just one of his five outings against the Sox, via a walk-off in extra innings in June.</p><p>“With the talented arms that the Guardians have, it is not just getting a good swing, you have to adjust,” said manager<b> Will Venable. </b>“You gotta find different ways to beat them.”</p><p>It gets worse: Williams failed to get through six innings in any of these outings, and an attempt to get him there Monday — facing the heart of the Sox’ order a third time — is where the game flipped in the visitors’ favor, giving the Sox a 4-3 win and a 2-0 edge in the best-of-five series.</p><p>Having already walked twice against Williams, <b>Miguel Vargas</b> worked a full count leading off the sixth inning before lining the seventh pitch he saw for a single. The hit chased Williams, who had entered the inning at 91 pitches, and kick-started the decisive three-run Sox rally against Guardians reliever <b>Erik Sabrowski</b>.</p><p>“[Williams] is a really good pitcher,” Vargas said. “My approach is focus on one pitch: middle-middle. I don’t think I’ve got much chance at anything else.”</p><p>Middle-middle is where the fastball Vargas singled on wound up being. He just had to make Williams work for a while.</p><p><b>Straight to the point for Taylor</b></p><p>After his four-inning outing in Game 1 on Saturday, it was up in the air whether reliever <b>Grant Taylor</b> would be physically able to pitch two days later. The answer came when he entered in the eighth inning Monday, weathering <b>Jo Adell</b>’s RBI triple to record a four-out save.</p><p>The conversation about his availability wound up being fairly short. Taylor said bench coach <b>Walker McKinven</b> approached him with a simple question: “You want it?”</p><p>“Obviously,” Taylor replied.</p><p><b>‘There’s hits in ice cream cones’</b></p><p>When <b>Sam Antonacci</b>, 23, told WGN on Sunday that he was eating an ice cream cone when Sox teammate <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> hit his two-run homer in Game  1, he noted he could have been in trouble with coaches if they’d needed him to pinch-hit and saw what he was doing.</p><p>But the Sox, with the youngest position-player group in the AL, see purpose in the snacks in the visitors’ clubhouse.</p><p>“I’ve noticed this in my baseball career: Ice cream cones are good luck,” said catcher<b> Kyle Teel</b>, 24. “There’s hits in ice cream cones.”</p><p>Venable has allowed his team to create their own clubhouse culture and stood by that approach in this case.</p><p>“I’m fully supportive of whatever these guys think is good luck,” Venable said. “Ice cream for everybody, then.”</p><p>Within reason at least. Antonacci–a lifelong infielder before this year–initially took a step in on Guardians outfielder <b>Steven Kwan</b>’s liner to left in the eighth, but held his focus to recover and make a scrambling catch for a crucial first out.</p><p>“Nice catch from Sam,” Vargas said. “I guess he wasn’t eating ice cream, so he made that play.”<br></p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: White Sox defy mistakes, expectations and physical limitations to take 2-0 lead in ALDS
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — In a pre-series scrum with White Sox beat writers last weekend, manager Will Venable warned that if the Sox yielded extra bases against the pesky American League Central-champion Guardians — be it through walks, errors or stolen bases — they’d lose.</p><p>By the time reliever Sean Newcomb’s throw to first skipped away in the first inning, allowing the Guardians to score two runs, the Sox had allowed the first two things to happen with only one out. It was yet another logical reason to expect them to come up short — or to fall back into the grim reality that defined most of their previous five years.</p><p>Instead, all the trouble melted away in a 4-3 victory in Game 2 of the ALDS.</p><p>When Brenton Doyle leaped at the wall to catch Patrick Bailey’s deep drive to center off Sox reliever Grant Taylor to end the game, the Sox were up 2-0 in the series, headed home for the first playoff game at Rate Field in five years and just one victory away from their first ALCS in 21 years.</p><p>“This is the identity of this team,” said infielder Miguel Vargas, who singled and scored in a decisive three-run sixth. “We know anybody here can have a huge at-bat and put us in the lead.”</p><p>Outfielder Braden Montgomery, a 2024 first-round draft pick by the Red Sox and a top-100 prospect, isn’t the most unlikely postseason hero after his two-out, two-run, go-ahead double off Guardians lefty Erik Sabrowski put the Sox up for good in the sixth. But Venable acknowledged before the game that Montgomery was a likely candidate to be replaced by a pinch-hitter against a left-hander after managing just a .430 OPS against lefties in the regular season.</p><p>Nevertheless, Montgomery prepared for Sabrowski like always and hit a first-pitch fastball down the right-field line in the sixth for one of the biggest Sox’ hits in years.</p><p>“He’s probably in the cage almost longer than anyone else,” Doyle said. “He really gives a crap about this game.”</p><p>It seemed questionable that Taylor would be available to pitch at all after logging four dominant innings to close out Game 1. As it turns out, he was slated to pitch one inning for a save if the situation came up, and he went one out longer than even that.</p><p>Three of his four outs were loud fly outs, wrapped around a booming triple by Joe Adell that reduced the Sox’ lead to a run. But style points aren’t what players concern themselves with in the playoff. Neither are whatever expectations this Sox team used to have.</p><p>A little over a year ago, Sean Burke was demoted to Triple-A Charlotte off a much weaker Sox roster. But on Monday, with midges swirling in the stadium in Cleveland, he picked up a game that threatened to spin out of control in the first and carried it until there were two outs in the eighth. He was pulled then after allowing his first hit in 5⅓ innings.</p><p>“I never thought the opponent would get a hit,” Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami boasted through his interpreter.</p><p>The Sox could have called an 84-win season a success without reaching the playoffs. Now they’re a win away from one of their deepest runs in franchise history. With a 36-45 road record this year, the Sox once looked like a team that needed their home environment to be successful. But four road playoff victories later, that has proven to be another misconception, another set of limitations to which the youngest group of position players in the league is not beholden.</p><p>For that, the young Sox have a hero’s welcome awaiting them in Chicago.</p><p>“I can’t place any expectations on it — I just know it’s going to be special,” Montgomery said of returning to their home field for Game 3 on Wednesday. “I can only imagine how the South Side is going to pop out in a couple of days. I can’t wait to see it and be a part of it.”</p>

entries.title: Police looking for man suspected of punching a woman on CTA platform
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are asking for help finding a man accused of punching a woman in the face on a South Loop CTA platform over the weekend.</p><p>The incident occurred at the Roosevelt CTA station about 11:55 a.m. on Sunday. The man is described as 35 to 40 years old, white or Hispanic and 5 feet 7 inches to 5 feet 10 inches tall. He was wearing a tan hooded sweatshirt, gray sweatpants and gray gym shoes without shoelaces. He has a thin mustache and short black hair, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information is asked to contact Mass Transit Detectives at 312-745-4447. Anonymous tips can be submitted at CPDTIP.com with the reference number RD JK-438007.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">AGGRAVATED BATTERY on <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/CTA?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#CTA</a> <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoCAPS01?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ChicagoCAPS01</a> (South Loop) <a href="https://x.com/Area3Detectives?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Area3Detectives</a> Mass Transit Detectives <a href="https://t.co/L8zuymcjqY">https://t.co/L8zuymcjqY</a> <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/ChicagoPolice?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#ChicagoPolice</a> <a href="https://t.co/HFLLXyObUY">pic.twitter.com/HFLLXyObUY</a></p>— Tom Ahern (@TAhern_) <a href="https://x.com/TAhern_/status/2107179509522759868?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: ‘She was a spark everywhere she went’ — Pilsen grieves one of its own
entries.summary: <p>Paola Judith Zamora Rojas' family gathered at her Pilsen apartment, as they have done many nights since her death.</p><p>Chairs faced an altar decorated with photographs of the 32-year-old mother. It was last Friday, the fourth evening of a nine-day Catholic novena.</p><p>Candles near the altar represented St. Jude. Zamora Rojas' older sister, Yahaira Gutierrez, said their mother, Sandra Zamora, prayed to the saint when Zamora Rojas stopped breathing during a near-death experience as a baby.</p><p>The family believes her survival was "some kind of miracle," Yahaira Gutierrez said. Sandra Zamora gave her daughter the middle name Judith in the saint's honor.</p><p>More than three decades later, St. Jude candles burned as the family prayed for her again.</p><p>Zamora Rojas had died by suicide Sept. 17 after what friends and relatives described as a long battle with mental illness.</p><p>Surrounding her family were traces of the life she had built: thrift-store records, vintage furniture and secondhand finds. Zamora Rojas' eye for fashion had earned her tens of thousands of followers on social media.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b00000" name="image-b00000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c440c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0b71aea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0e478d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Paola Judith Zamora Rojas' mother, Sandra Zamora, places her daughter’s portrait on the wall during a prayer vigil for her daughter on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. Zamora Rojas died by suicide in September 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0e478d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3d01754/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0e478d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F23%2F0366eb2447d484fb3e1e84493e2a%2Fpaolavigil-261003-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Paola Judith Zamora Rojas’ mother, Sandra Zamora, places her daughter’s portrait on the wall during a prayer vigil for her daughter on Friday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Octavio Jones/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Also attending was Diana Galicia Corona, whose son, Gabriel Cisneros, had been Zamora Rojas' fiancé .</p><p>Zamora Rojas was three months pregnant with their daughter, Olivia, when Cisneros, 22, died of an accidental heroin overdose on Mother's Day in 2016. She continued to call Galicia Corona her mother-in-law afterward. Galicia Corona said she called Zamora Rojas a "better-in-law."</p><p>A week before Cisneros died, Galicia Corona remembers leaving a Pilsen restaurant with the couple when music began playing, and her son took Zamora Rojas' hand, spun her around and danced with her on the sidewalk.</p><p>"What Gabriel and Paola had was a love story that should have never ended," Galicia Corona said.</p><p>Zamora Rojas never stopped grieving him, her family said. Galicia Corona saw that grief resurface around his birthday, holidays and the anniversary of his death.</p><p>Grief and depression were only parts of a life her family said was remarkably full.</p><p>Zamora Rojas was raising a daughter she adored, reselling clothing online, attending concerts and hosting traveling musicians in her home.</p><p>She showed new friends around Chicago and supported Pilsen artists and businesses, her family said.</p><p>And she often was the person others turned to when they were struggling.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Another said Zamora Rojas offered financial help despite her own money struggles.</p><p>"I want to make sure people know that Paola wasn't selfish," Yahaira Gutierrez said.</p><p>Yahaira Gutierrez said her sister worried about burdening others, sometimes keeping her pain to herself.</p><p></p><p>Zamora Rojas moved to Pilsen with her family when she was 2 or 3, Yahaira Gutierrez said. While their mother worked, the kids knew which neighbors they could call for help.</p><p>"Pilsen grew in her," Yahaira Gutierrez said. "And that's how she grew into Pilsen."</p><p>As an adult, shopping locally became part of her identity, friends and family said. </p><p>“A lot of her stuff is from somewhere else,” her brother, Cesar Gutierrez said, laughing about the phone calls he received from her asking for help moving furniture she found or thrifted. “You know how you usually go to Target and buy something brand new? She wouldn't go to Target.”</p><p>Zamora Rojas began thrifting as a child and later worked at Pilsen Vintage, where co-owners Paul Guizar and Maggie Reynoso said she was family.</p><p>She later sold her finds through <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/deadendvintagechicago?stkn=MWhjczY3dmplNHBwaQ==" target="_blank" >an Instagram account called Dead End Vintage</a>, modeling the clothing herself.</p><p>Galicia Corona said they dreamed of opening a Pilsen cafe that would double as a thrift store. entries.title: White Sox hold on for victory over Guardians to take 2-0 lead in ALDS showdown
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — In a pre-series scrum with White Sox beat writers last weekend, manager Will Venable warned that if the Sox yielded extra bases against the pesky American League Central-champion Guardians — be it through walks, errors or stolen bases — they’d lose.</p><p>By the time reliever Sean Newcomb’s throw to first skipped away in the first inning, allowing the Guardians to score two runs, the Sox had allowed the first two things to happen with only one out. It was yet another logical reason to expect them to come up short — or to fall back into the grim reality that defined most of their previous five years.</p><p>Instead, all the trouble melted away in a 4-3 victory in Game 2 of the ALDS.</p><p>When Brenton Doyle leaped at the wall to catch Patrick Bailey’s deep drive to center off Sox reliever Grant Taylor to end the game, the Sox were up 2-0 in the series, headed home for the first playoff game at Rate Field in five years and just one victory away from their first ALCS in 21 years.</p><p>“This is the identity of this team,” said infielder Miguel Vargas, who singled and scored in a decisive three-run sixth. “We know anybody here can have a huge at-bat and put us in the lead.”</p><p>Outfielder Braden Montgomery, a 2024 first-round draft pick by the Red Sox and a top-100 prospect, isn’t the most unlikely postseason hero after his two-out, two-run, go-ahead double off Guardians lefty Erik Sabrowski put the Sox up for good in the sixth. But Venable acknowledged before the game that Montgomery was a likely candidate to be replaced by a pinch-hitter against a left-hander after managing just a .430 OPS against lefties in the regular season.</p><p>Nevertheless, Montgomery prepared for Sabrowski like always and hit a first-pitch fastball down the right-field line in the sixth for one of the biggest Sox’ hits in years.</p><p>“He’s probably in the cage almost longer than anyone else,” Doyle said. “He really gives a crap about this game.”</p><p>It seemed questionable that Taylor would be available to pitch at all after logging four dominant innings to close out Game 1. As it turns out, he was slated to pitch one inning for a save if the situation came up, and he went one out longer than even that.</p><p>Three of his four outs were loud fly outs, wrapped around a booming triple by Joe Adell that reduced the Sox’ lead to a run. But style points aren’t what players concern themselves with in the playoff. Neither are whatever expectations this Sox team used to have.</p><p>A little over a year ago, Sean Burke was demoted to Triple-A Charlotte off a much weaker Sox roster. But on Monday, with midges swirling in the stadium in Cleveland, he picked up a game that threatened to spin out of control in the first and carried it until there were two outs in the eighth. He was pulled then after allowing his first hit in 5⅓ innings.</p><p>“I never thought the opponent would get a hit,” Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami boasted through his interpreter.</p><p>The Sox could have called an 84-win season a success without reaching the playoffs. Now they’re a win away from one of their deepest runs in franchise history. With a 36-45 road record this year, the Sox once looked like a team that needed their home environment to be successful. But four road playoff victories later, that has proven to be another misconception, another set of limitations to which the youngest group of position players in the league is not beholden.</p><p>For that, the young Sox have a hero’s welcome awaiting them in Chicago.</p><p>“I can’t place any expectations on it — I just know it’s going to be special,” Montgomery said of returning to their home field for Game 3 on Wednesday. “I can only imagine how the South Side is going to pop out in a couple of days. I can’t wait to see it and be a part of it.”<br></p>

entries.title: Braden Montgomery shows he belongs with biggest hit of his life in White Sox' victory
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — Braden Montgomery didn’t have a great rookie season at the plate. It started magically in June with a walk-off home run in his major-league debut to beat the Braves, the best team in baseball at the time.</p><p>He had two doubles the next night in another White Sox victory against the Braves. Their No. 2 prospect — the 21st-ranked in baseball — was on a path to stardom.</p><p>But the rest of his season was mostly nondescript. Although he was good with the glove, he left a lot to be desired with the bat. He hit six homers in 93 games, lacking the pop he showed at Texas A&M, where he hit 27 homers in 61 games in 2024. He finished the regular season with a paltry .662 OPS.</p><p>Manager Will Venable kept putting him in the lineup, though, even into the postseason. Entering Game 2 of the American League Division Series against the Guardians on Monday, he was hitless in his last 10 at-bats.</p><p>The question had to be asked: Why is he in the lineup?</p><p>So a reporter worked up the nerve to ask Venable a question he probably wouldn’t like, and he asked it in the most ham-handed of ways:</p><p>“Braden Montgomery is in the lineup every day. What makes you confident that he belongs in the lineup every day?”</p><p>“Are you thinking he shouldn’t be in the lineup?” Venable replied.</p><p>As a matter of fact, that’s exactly what I thought . . . I mean, what the reporter thought. His name has been removed to protect his family.</p><p>“No, no, no,” the reporter said, backtracking as sweat began to pool on his forehead. “I just want to know what you think makes him so valuable for a rookie?”</p><p>“Oh, gotcha. Braden is a special player.”</p><p>Venable went on, talking about Montgomery being a valuable switch hitter, a really good defender, a great athlete, a “big piece of our lineup.”</p><p>Having seemingly spoken it into existence, Venable watched as Montgomery had the biggest hit of his life, a go-ahead, two-run double in the sixth inning that helped give the Sox a 4-3 victory and a 2-0 lead in the series, which could end Wednesday at Rate Field.</p><p>Facing left-handed reliever Erik Sabrowski, the switch-hitting Montgomery — who hit .129 right-handed against lefties during the regular season — lined a first-pitch fastball low and away down the line in right field, landing it maybe a foot inside the line. Miguel Vargas and Randal Grichuk scored, and when Montgomery reached second base, he let out a yell that every Sox fan felt.</p><p>“I can’t even describe the energy that was running through me in that moment,” Montgomery said. “To see the ball get down and to know you’ve got two ducks on the pond that are right there, it’s exhilarating. It was special to touch the bag and look back into the dugout and see my guys. It’s a feeling like no other. You want to feel that feeling every night.”</p><p>What is it that makes Venable so confident in Montgomery, despite what the numbers say?</p><p>“He’s a guy that is not going to shy away from the moment,” Venable said. “As you’re evaluating your best nine on a given day, it’s not just what happens at the plate. It’s defensive ability. It’s baserunning. Really, everything.”</p><p>Montgomery doesn’t take that confidence for granted.</p><p>“It’s really special for me, coming from a person like Will,” he said. “Getting to know Will and seeing the man that he is, I respect him so much. To have that confidence in me means the world. I feel like that makes winning ballclubs, when you create these bonds with people. I’d run through a wall for Will.”</p><p>OK, so I was wrong. I mean, the reporter was wrong. Montgomery, who shows a maturity beyond his years, belongs in the lineup every day.</p><p>Now the Sox come home, where they’ll be greeted by a raucous crowd that hasn’t seen them since Sept. 27, when they beat the Rockies in a meaningless regular-season finale. They had lost the night before, and the Guardians had won, clinching the AL Central title. That the Guardians lost the next day to make the final margin just one game was awfully nervy.</p><p>But the Sox could end up having the last laugh with a series sweep — or just a series victory. It’s called the regular season because it’s regular; it’s normal. What Montgomery and the Sox are doing in the postseason is anything but.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Husband struggles to manage wife's dementia and hoarding
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> As an 80-year-old man, I'm up against a problem I cannot deal with. I've been married to an amazing lady for 57 years whom I love to death. She has put up with a lot from me, and I am so grateful. Now it's my turn, and I'm falling woefully short. Her mother died of complications from dementia, as did her older brother. My mother had it as well. We had always lived some distance from them, so we didn't see firsthand the trials and tribulations they went through daily, just the end result.</p><p>My wife was diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment a few years ago. I was able to get her enrolled in a clinical trial they had hoped would arrest its progress, but it didn't. She can no longer be trusted to drive, having totaled her car a few years ago.</p><p>Along with dementia, she is now a hoarder. She will not throw anything away. When I suggest we hire some help, she acts like I'm throwing her out on the street. I have no friends and very few acquaintances between doing all the grocery shopping, keeping the house repaired, driving her to doctor appointments, etc. I recently joined a fitness gym that I have used only twice.</p><p>My wife's two sisters live hundreds of miles from us and have somewhat impaired husbands of their own. Our three grown sons think she is not too bad, and only two live within an hour of us. For her sake, my only options are not good. — <i>BEWILDERED IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR BEWILDERED:</b> You have my sympathy as you deal with this heartbreaking condition. The most important thing to remember is that if you don't take care of yourself, there will be no one to take care of your wife. That means if you need to hire help, you must do so, regardless of your wife's feelings on the matter. At the very least, have someone come in to look after her so you can shop and use that gym membership a few times each week. The stronger your body is, the better you'll be able to care for your wife.</p><p>I urge you to visit the Alzheimer's Association at alz.org or call the 24-hour helpline at 1-800-272-3900. They have a wealth of information and resources for caregivers. You may have more options than you think.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband yawns loudly over and over when we are watching TV in the evening. I have asked him to please not be so loud when he yawns, and he gets annoyed that I asked. He still yawns loudly many times a day. How do I get him to stop making a production of his yawning? — <i>BLASTED OUT IN IDAHO</i></p><p><b>DEAR BLASTED OUT:</b> Folks have been known to yawn excessively because they aren't getting enough oxygen or suffer from sleep apnea. I doubt your husband does this just to annoy you. It might benefit him to mention all that yawning to his physician in case it needs to be checked out.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: 2026 Chicago Marathon — what to know, how to watch
entries.summary: <p>It's a weather day — good or bad — that will be cemented into thousands of memories perhaps even more than one's wedding day.</p><p>It will determine heaps for the record 55,000 plus runners headed to the starting line in Grant Park Sunday to amble, dash and jog their way to the finish line of the 48th Bank of America Chicago Marathon.</p><p>With just under a week to go, meteorologists at the National Weather Service predict a dry and partially sunny day with temperatures that will start in the 50s and climb into the mid-70s by the afternoon — in other words, good marathon weather.</p><p>"It's still subject to change, but right now, especially at the start of the race, it looks like it will be really nice weather out there," said NWS meteorologist Jake Petr.</p><p>The marathon is part of the Abbott World Marathon Majors, a series of eight of the largest and most renowned marathons in the world. The course closes at 4 p.m.</p><h3><b>Street closures</b></h3><p>Most streets along the marathon route will close to traffic at 6 a.m. Sunday, with many streets remaining closed to traffic until 4 p.m. Race organizers suggest using expressways, including DuSable Lakeshore Drive, to traverse the area and avoid street closures. Expect bus reroutes from 6 a.m. through 4 p.m. on routes that normally pass through the race area. second-fastest ever run by an American. Top American women include Susanna Sullivan and Natosha Rogers.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>While Kenyan Sabastian Sawe — who set the world record with the sport's first official sub-two hour marathon of 1:59:30 in London this spring — will not be running due to injury, the men's field is still stacked with competitors seeking to write their own names in the record books.</p><p>Chief among them is Ugandan Jacob Kiplimo, who finished just 58 seconds behind Sawe in London with a time of 2:00:28 — the third-fastest marathon time ever.</p><p>Homegrown talent to keep an eye on includes rising American star Charles Hicks, whose time of 2:04:35 at the Boston Marathon this year is the second-fastest ever run by an American.</p><p>On the women's side, Kenyan Ruth Chepngetich, who set a women’s world record in Chicago in 2024 with a time of 2:09:56, is sidelined again this year because of a three-year suspension due to a positive doping test. In her absence, a top favorite is Brigid Kosgei, of Kenya, whose best marathon time of 2:14:04 came when she won Chicago in 2019. Hawi Feysa, of Ethiopia, is another contender. Her best time of 2:14:56 came when she won in Chicago last year.</p><p>Top American women include Susanna Sullivan and Natosha Rogers. Both set their personal bests in Chicago. Sullivan's came in 2024 with a time of 2:21:56. The best time for Rogers came last year with a finish of 2:23:28.</p>

The set feels like a haunted house.</p><p>And while the 1990 Broadway show didn’t catch on, the local version has been a huge success, and director Derek Van Barham has an idea why that’s happened.</p><p>“We are able to capture the big huge gothic sound, but instead of playing in a huge 2,500 seat theater, it's like right on top of the audience,” he said. “I think something about that mix of the melodrama and the heightened style and just ballad after ballad being right there, and having the ability to just blow people's hair back — this is the perfect container for all that.”</p><p>Comic thriller, haunted puppets — fright takes many forms on Chicago stages this fall. The structure of part coming-of-age and part true-crime, come from the real life interests of Pharel. She loves the “Murder with my Husband” podcast, and also knows the importance of friendship in adolescent girls.</p><p>“I was interested in the ways young women save each other," she said. Her original inspiration came from her relationship with her best friend, and from there moved to a scary reality: “What is really behind this obsession with true crime? I know part of it for me is that I want to feel prepared when I'm in a situation, and so what are the anxieties that these young women expect? Why do young Black and brown girls really go missing? Michigan Ave., tickets from $31</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8f0000" name="module-8f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Your guide to fall culture in Chicago </b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-f6c56c02-ac5f-11f1-988e-bd5e5ce8e98f"><li>The next big thing is happening on Chicago’s small stages. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/things-to-do/2026/09/04/theater-to-see-chicago-fall-storefront-tickets-new-plays-musicals" target="_blank" ><u>Here are 10 plays and musicals</u></a> not to miss this theater season.</li><li>The ultimate guide to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/movies-tv/2026/09/10/chicago-fall-film-festivals-events-things-to-do-movies-ciff-cuff-reeling" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago’s fall film festivals</u></a>, from Oscar contenders to local standouts</li><li>Evanston’s $32 million <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/09/03/evanston-northlight-theater-chicago-suburbs-arts-annex" target="_blank" ><u>new Northlight Theatre</u></a> wasn’t built for big crowds. It’s built for new plays.</li><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/09/08/mary-cassatt-after-impressionism-art-institute-chicago-paintings-impressionist-mural-worlds-fair-1893" target="_blank" ><u>“Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism”</u></a> is the Art Institute’s first deep-dive into Cassatt in more than 25 years and explores some of her historical Chicago ties.</li><li>There’s action in Chicago’s art galleries. entries.title: ‘Divergent’ author Veronica Roth returns with a new twist on her bestselling series – on her own terms
entries.summary: <p>The line for a Veronica Roth book signing can snake down a hallway. It did on a recent weeknight at Navy Pier as Chicago fans clutched their books, some with worn edges, and waited to meet the famous local author.</p><p>Fifteen years ago, “Divergent” turned Roth into a bestselling author, landing at No. 1 on the New York Times Bestseller list and turning into a successful movie starring Shailene Woodley as its heroine, Tris. At Navy Pier, readers who discovered the series in their adolescence waited in anticipation to meet Roth, whose new book “The Sixth Faction,” out Tuesday, brings readers back to the world that made her famous while also changing one of the key decisions in the story.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" class="Form-newsletter-wrapper" target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>“Divergent” brought Roth a literary fame, but also a load of criticism that the author, who still lives in Chicago, has struggled to make sense of. She said she wrote her new book to release a weight.</p><p>“I had kind of carried around a lot of negativity about the series in the last 15 years. The way to lighten that load was to make something new,” Roth said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/books/2026/10/01/new-books-to-read-recommendations-fall-2026" >10 new books to read this fall with a Chicago flair</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“Divergent” is set in a futuristic Chicago that divides society into five factions built around virtues – Abnegation (The Selfless), Amity (The Peaceful), Candor (The Honest), Dauntless (The Brace) and Erudite (The Intelligent). Every 16-year-old must choose one.</p><p>Beatrice Prior, nicknamed Tris, originally picks Dauntless, where she learns to become a brave risk taker, jumping trains, rushing into frightful situations like volunteering to be a human target during a knife-throwing training. In “The Sixth Faction,” Roth designs an alternate universe with the same characters and Chicago setting. But something tragic happens at Tris’s choosing ceremony, and her life takes a completely different course.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> The way to lighten that load was to make something new,” Roth said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Barry Brecheisen for the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>For Roth, the “Divergent” series was the fulfillment of a dream. Its success gave her the career she’d dreamed of since her childhood, allowing her to pursue only passion projects.</p><p>While she said this freedom was invaluable, with widespread recognition came widespread criticism. She said many people reading dystopian fiction are looking for a critique of contemporary society, but that she didn’t intend for “Divergent” to read that way. Additionally, the original series concluded in a controversial way that upset many readers.</p><p>“I wasn’t prepared for the scale of it. I was really young,” said Roth, who was in her early 20s when “Divergent” debuted. “I wasn’t quite emotionally or mentally prepared for that much negativity in my life, and so I really sucked it in like a sponge, and that’s what I’ve had to unlearn.”</p><p>Roth credits therapy with helping her challenge the belief that negative criticism must be true simply because it hurts to hear. She has written at least 10 more books since “Divergent” was published in 2011. In addition to understanding how to emotionally handle criticism, she’s learned some practical things as a writer over the years.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4a0000" name="image-4a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c4965b6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+164/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2F43%2F95047259498ea469beb81ce0f819%2Frothbook-261004-010.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d25f0ed/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+164/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2F43%2F95047259498ea469beb81ce0f819%2Frothbook-261004-010.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/522af1c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+164/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2F43%2F95047259498ea469beb81ce0f819%2Frothbook-261004-010.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="In center, author Veronica Roth with fellow book enthusiasts during “A Celebration of The Sixth Faction” at Navy Pier in Chicago, IL on Wednesday, August 12, 2026. But then I got to the third book, 'Allegiant,' and I realized I had set some things up that I was gonna have a hard time figuring out, and so after doing that, I was like, never again.”</p><p>Roth said her approach to writing changed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Reflecting on her own mortality made the author want to enjoy her work everyday.</p><p>“I need to worry less about other people and worry more about the joy and fulfillment of writing,” she said.</p><h3><b>Fans with their own “what if?”s</b></h3><p>At the Navy Pier signing, several fans said the alternate-universe concept struck a personal chord.</p><p>“I feel like the older I get, the more I'm asking myself, well, what if I did this instead? What if I chose that instead?” Hadeel Abderrhaman said. “Going back to a series that I loved as a child and being like, ‘Wait, like we actually get to see what if she chose differently?’”</p><p>Abderrhaman said she’s read every book in the series every year for 15 years.</p><p>Another fan, Dania Amora, discovered the series at her school’s Scholastic Book Fair when she entries.title: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker lost 80 pounds with help from GLP-1 medications. What are they?
entries.summary: <p>In a September <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/09/21/illinois-governor-jb-pritzker-interview-glp-1-diabetes-weight-loss" target="_blank" ><u>Sun-Times interview</u></a>, Gov. JB Pritzker revealed he has lost 80 pounds since spring 2024 with help from a GLP-1 medication. His doctor first diagnosed him with prediabetes. Later, when Pritzker was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes, he began taking insulin — and ultimately an undisclosed GLP-1 drug.</p><p>The medication — combined with exercise and diet — has been so effective that Pritzker, 61, stopped taking insulin nine months ago, and his blood sugar levels are normal, he said. Pritzker plans to continue to lose weight.</p><p>The governor said he wanted to talk openly about his weight loss journey, largely in part because he knows millions of Americans are suffering from obesity-related health conditions. The disclosure also comes just months before Democrats are expected to announce their intentions for president. For now, Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/09/pritzker-for-president-handicapping-the-illinois-governors-political-future" target="_blank" ><u>said he’s focusing</u></a> on winning his third term for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/09/pritzker-for-president-handicapping-the-illinois-governors-political-future" target="_blank" ><u>governor</u></a> in November.</p><p><b>What are GLP-1s?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/04/30/weight-loss-drug-coverage-illinois-state-workers-taxpayers-price-tag" target="_blank" ><u>GLP-1s</u></a> are a class of drugs, known as GLP-1 receptor agonists, that mainly help manage blood sugar levels in people with Type 2 diabetes, according to Cleveland Clinic. Some GLP-1 agonists can also help treat obesity and promote weight loss. Well-known brands include Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound.</p><p>To learn more about how GLP-1s work, look to sources such as healthcare providers such as <a class="Link" href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/13901-glp-1-agonists" target="_blank" ><u>Cleveland Clinic</u></a> and Mayo Clinic and medical experts from <a class="Link" href="https://med.stanford.edu/news/insights/2026/06/glp1s-101-weight-loss-wegovy-ozempic-zepbound-side-effects-safe-use.html" target="_blank" ><u>Stanford</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.tuftsmedicine.org/about-us/news/beyond-scale-your-guide-glp-1s" target="_blank" ><u>Tufts</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.health.harvard.edu/healthy-aging-and-longevity/how-does-ozempic-work-understanding-glp-1s-for-diabetes-weight-loss-and-beyond" target="_blank" ><u>Harvard</u></a>. They also detail the benefits, risks and side effects of GLP-1s.</p><p><b>Who might be eligible for GLP-1s? </b></p><p>Generally, GLP-1s are approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for adults aged 18 years and older with certain body mass indexes, typically 30 or above.</p><p>Those with a BMI of 27 or above could be eligible if they have a weight-related health condition such as hypertension, high cholesterol, weight-related anxiety, liver disease, sleep apnea or polycystic ovary syndrome, according to pharmacy chain <a class="Link" href="https://www.walgreens.com/topic/virtual-healthcare/weight-loss.jsp" target="_blank" ><u>Walgreens</u></a>.</p><p>People with BMI of 27 or higher who are <a class="Link" href="https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/weight-loss-drugs" target="_blank" ><u>prediabetic</u></a>, had a previous heart attack, stroke, or have blocked arteries in their legs or arms with symptoms might also be eligible.</p><p>Healthcare providers may also prescribe GLP-1s for people who are overweight, along with other health conditions, if losing weight can help manage the coexisting conditions, according to <a class="Link" href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/13901-glp-1-agonists" target="_blank" ><u>Cleveland Clinic</u></a>.<a class="Link" href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/overweight" target="_blank" ><u>Overweight</u></a> is generally a BMI of 25 to 29.9. Asians with a BMI of 23 or higher may have an increased risk of health problems, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/obesity/symptoms-causes/syc-20375742" target="_blank" ><u>Mayo Clinic</u></a>.</p><p><b>Will health insurance cover GLP-1s?</b></p><p>Coverage depends on your medical eligibility and health insurance. Insurance often covers GLP-1s for treating Type 2 diabetes. Most plans typically do not cover GLP-1s for weight loss alone.</p><p>Whether insurance will cover the cost of GLP-1s can be complicated, depending on eligibility and types of coverage.</p><p>Coverage also varies by state. In Illinois, eligible state workers are covered by insurance.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/04/30/weight-loss-drug-coverage-illinois-state-workers-taxpayers-price-tag" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois expanded coverage</u></a> for eligible state workers in July 2023 under the state’s group health insurance program. (Pritzker started taking GLP-1 injections in spring 2024.)</p><p>GLP-1 coverage was previously available for state workers diagnosed with diabetes — but the expansion covered the drug for weight loss.</p><p>The state’s expanded coverage cost $147 million in fiscal year 2025. The high cost has been criticized, but officials say there are benefits in the long run.</p><p>“By adding coverage for injectable weight loss medications to state health insurance plans, more people will have a chance to eliminate long-term health problems,” Cathy Kwiatkowski, Illinois Department of Central Management Services spokesperson, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/04/30/weight-loss-drug-coverage-illinois-state-workers-taxpayers-price-tag" target="_blank" ><u>told the Sun-Times.</u></a></p><p>She said people on the state program with prediabetes, gestational diabetes or obesity are eligible for the drugs if “deemed medically appropriate by the physician,” and enrollees have to participate in a “lifestyle management program.”</p><p>Notably, Medicaid in Illinois covers GLP-1s with a Type 2 diabetes diagnosis but not for weight loss.</p><p><b>If insurance doesn’t cover GLP-1s, can you pay out of pocket? If so, how much can the medication cost?</b></p><p>It’s possible to pay out of pocket for a prescription. It’s best to discuss options with a medical expert and health insurer.</p><p>Self-pay options vary. For example, the list price for all dosages of Ozempic pens and pills is $1,027.51, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.novocare.com/diabetes/products/ozempic/explaining-list-price.html" target="_blank" ><u>Novocare</u></a>, part of drugmaker Novo Nordisk, which makes Ozempic. (Monthly dosage depends on the individual.) List price is the manufacturer’s original price before any discounts. But most people don’t pay the list price if they have health insurance, according to Novocare’s website.</p><p>Purchasing GLP-1s from the manufacturer may be cheaper. For example, Novo Nordisk offers the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wegovy.com/obesity/what-to-pay-for-wegovy.html" target="_blank" ><u>Wegovy</u></a> pill for $149 to $299 per month, depending on dosage. Its injectable pen costs up to $399 per month.</p><p>Pharmaceutical company <a class="Link" href="https://www.lilly.com/lillydirect/zepbound" target="_blank" ><u>Eli Lilly</u></a> offers Zepbound for $299 to $449 per month, depending on dosage.</p><p>For a ballpark estimate, Weight Watchers has an online GLP-1 <a class="Link" href="https://www.weightwatchers.com/us/weight-loss-medication/cost-estimator?cid%3DsemWW_google-_psearch_clini-CostEstimator_us-en_sus_bau_psp-x-brand-all-_-__-_20260212___10027weight+watchers+glp+1+cost%26account%3DWWUS%26tracker%3D2161590738239$$=&g_acctid=243-229-0722&g_adgroupid=193443888139&g_adid=813340696450&g_adtype=search&g_campaign=WW-Generic%7CControllingTerms%7CExact%2BPhrase_google-_psearch_clini__us-en_sus_bau_psp-x-brand__20260212__&g_campaignid=23564177008&g_keyword=weight%20watchers%20glp%201%20cost&g_keywordid=kwd-2161590738239&g_network=g&utm_campaign=WW-Generic%7CControllingTerms%7CExact%2BPhrase_google-_psearch_clini__us-en_sus_bau_psp-x-brand__20260212__&utm_content=WW_google-_psearch_clini-CostEstimator_us-en_sus_bau_psp-x-brand-all-_-__-_20260212___10027&utm_medium=cpc&utm_source=google&utm_term=weight%20watchers%20glp%201%20cost&gclsrc=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23564177008&gbraid=0AAAAADHsUeWh49Yszz6ViH3Ew8IYE7aY-&gclid=CjwKCAjwifjVBhBKEiwAYx4K9IvBAAibZuYyPq08jLcTn9_8bFyFE3VkIZtEoACEIusQ7AulPnV0MBoCN8YQAvD_BwE" target="_blank" ><u>cost calculator.</u></a> It gives an estimate based on your height, weight, health insurance provider and type of GLP-1 medication.</p><p><b>Are there health risks to GLP-1s?</b></p><p>Yes. Anyone considering GLP-1s should consult a medical expert.</p><p>According to healthcare providers <a class="Link" href="https://healthy.kaiserpermanente.org/health-wellness/healtharticle.weight-loss-drugs" target="_blank" ><u>Kaiser Permanente</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/type-2-diabetes/expert-answers/byetta/faq-20057955" target="_blank" ><u>Mayo Clinic</u></a>, GLP-1s may not be right for people with a history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (a type of thyroid cancer) or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (tumors in endocrine glands), for those with a history of disordered eating and during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.</p><p>Potential <a class="Link" href="https://med.stanford.edu/news/insights/2026/06/glp1s-101-weight-loss-wegovy-ozempic-zepbound-side-effects-safe-use.html" target="_blank" ><u>side effects</u></a> include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation and acid reflux, as well as higher risk of bowel obstructions and pancreatitis. GLP-1s may increase depression and risk for suicide.</p><p>GLP-1s are relatively new, with the FDA approving the first one in 2005, said <a class="Link" href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/13901-glp-1-agonists" target="_blank" ><u>Cleveland Clinic</u></a>. Researchers are still learning about them. “Until more long-term studies are done, the risk to humans isn't known,” said <a class="Link" href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/type-2-diabetes/expert-answers/byetta/faq-20057955" target="_blank" ><u>Mayo Clinic</u></a>.</p><p><b>What are other risks?</b></p><p>This year, about 11% of U.S. adults — nearly 30 million people – are taking GLP-1s for weight loss purposes, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/712157/glp-usage-reaches-new-high.aspx" target="_blank" ><u>Gallup</u></a> survey this summer. That’s a big jump from 3% in 2024.</p><p>With high demand comes misuse and more unapproved versions of the drugs.</p><p>Illinois Attorney General <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisattorneygeneral.gov/news/story/updated-consumer-alertattorney-general-raoul-reminds-illinois-residents-to-be-vigilant-when-seeking-glp-1-drugs-for-weight-loss" target="_blank" ><u>Kwame Raoul</u></a> last year warned about sellers offering potentially harmful unapproved versions of GLP-1s. He urged consumers to get prescriptions from reputable health care providers and to fill prescriptions at licensed pharmacies.</p><p>Raoul warned consumers about “misleading advertising by med spas, wellness centers, online retailers and social media sellers” offering compounded drugs not approved by the FDA.</p><p>The FDA has also raised concerns about unapproved versions of GLP-1s. The agency’s list of <a class="Link" href="https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fdas-concerns-unapproved-glp-1-drugs-used-weight-loss" target="_blank" ><u>red flags</u></a> includes sellers that offer medicine at “deep discounts or prices that seem too good to be true” or don’t require a screening and prescription by a licensed doctor.</p><p>In the rush to use GLP-1s, more people are misusing and overdosing on medication, as well as using unapproved versions without prescriptions.</p><p>In just one year, calls to Illinois poison centers for overdoses or side effects of injectable weight loss drugs have more than doubled, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/calls-to-poison-centers-skyrocket-amid-rise-in-use-of-glp-1-drugs/3970572/" target="_blank" ><u>NBC Chicago</u></a> in August.</p><p>Nationwide, <a class="Link" href="https://poisoncenters.org/track/GLP-1" target="_blank" ><u>Poison Centers</u></a> have seen a nearly 1,500% increase in calls since 2019 related to overdose or side effects of injectable weight-loss drugs. Poison Centers represents the 53 accredited poison control centers in the U.S.</p><p>Quality problems with any medications can be reported to the FDA’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.fda.gov/safety/medwatch-fda-safety-information-and-adverse-event-reporting-program" target="_blank" ><u>MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting</u></a> program.</p>

entries.title: Fiscal general y Ciudad de Chicago buscan poner fin a olores ‘repugnantes’ de una planta en el lado sureste
entries.summary: <p>Funcionarios estatales y municipales están pidiendo a un juez de la Corte de Circuito del Condado de Cook que suspenda las operaciones en Pullman Innovations, que ha sido el origen de cientos de quejas por malos olores pútridos.</p><p>El fiscal general de Illinois, Kwame Raoul, y abogados de la Ciudad quieren que el juez obligue a Pullman a cerrar mientras la empresa diseña un plan para controlar los olores. La empresa fabrica un aditivo para alimento animal que usan agricultores que suministran huevos a la empresa alimentaria Dutch Farms.</p><p>Raoul y la Ciudad demandaron a la empresa en agosto por los olores, alegando violaciones de las leyes estatales y municipales sobre contaminación del aire.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2a0000" name="module-2a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La moción incluyó numerosos testimonios, entre ellos el de un exempleado que dijo que su ropa “olía a muerte” después de un turno.</p><p>“La empresa no debería poder continuar operando hasta que atienda los olores y la contaminación del aire, y garantice que sus operaciones cumplan con las leyes ambientales de Illinois”, dijo Raoul en un comunicado.</p><p>No se pudo localizar a un abogado de Pullman para obtener comentarios.</p><p>Algunos vecinos sugirieron al Chicago Sun-Times en agosto que el olor pudo haber enmascarado el hedor de cuerpos en descomposición en la funeraria South Chicago Chapel, ahora bajo investigación.</p><p>Pullman Innovations, en 2701 E. 100th St., está a aproximadamente una milla de la funeraria. Sin embargo, la dirección del viento puede arrastrar el olor por toda la zona más amplia del vecindario de South Deering, en el extremo sureste de la ciudad.</p><p>La planta de aditivos para alimento animal ha sido durante mucho tiempo fuente de quejas por molestias que se remontan décadas atrás a una empresa predecesora, Agri-Fine, que anteriormente fue demandada por la exfiscal general Lisa Madigan antes de cerrar.</p><p>Pullman, constituida como A-F Acquisition, compró la planta y sus activos en 2016.</p><p>Los residentes estuvieron en guerra con Agri-Fine por los olores durante más de 20 años, hasta que la empresa se acogió a la protección por bancarrota hace más de una década.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Driver dead in rollover crash on Chinatown feeder ramp
entries.summary: <p>A driver died in a rollover crash early Tuesday on the Chinatown feeder ramp just off of the Stevenson Expressway, authorities said.</p><p>The crash happened around 1:15 a.m. on the ramp from the northbound lanes of Interstate 55, according to Illinois state police. </p><p>The vehicle struck a guardrail before hitting a light pole and rolling over, state police said in a statement. </p><p>The driver was taken to a hospital and pronounced dead, officials said. The person's name was not released. </p>

entries.title: Reality TV star and luxury broker Ryan Serhant opening Chicago outpost
entries.summary: <p>Serhant, the real estate brokerage firm founded by reality TV star Ryan Serhant, is expanding to Chicago.</p><p>The brokerage said Tuesday it will serve Chicago and the North Shore. It has plans for an office in the North Shore area, but for now is in temporary space in Wicker Park.</p><p>Ryan Serhant, a long-time real estate broker, became famous on Bravo's reality TV series "Million Dollar Listing: New York," leaving after nine seasons. He later starred in and produced Netflix's "Owning Manhattan," which follows Serhant and his New York-based brokerage as they sell luxury homes. </p><p>He launched his namesake firm in 2020. In 2024, the company launched an in-house AI platform called S.MPLE. It allows agents to access to AI-powered tools for lead generation, marketing and transaction management. The firm also has more than 11 million followers across its social media platforms, touting itself as the most followed real estate brand in the world. </p><p>"Real estate in Chicago has run the same way for a long time,” Serhant said in a news release. “Agents here are ready for something built for how buyers and sellers actually live today, and through S.MPLE, we're giving them the AI, technology and reach to lead that change.”</p><p>Serhant Illinois' office is launching with four founders, who come from @properties and Jameson Sotheby's International Realty. Dina Lissner, previously managing broker for Baird & Warner's Highland Park office, will serve as managing director of Serhant Illinois.</p><p>"Everything I've done in my career, from the classroom to wellness to running a brokerage, has come back to helping people grow, and that's what I'm most excited to do here," Lissner said. "Chicago and the North Shore have some of the most talented agents in the country, and Serhant gives them something no one else can: the technology, the media and a brand that puts them in front of the world. I'm thrilled to be building this from the ground up with agents who are ready for what's next."</p><p>The office will have more than 40 agents and plans to grow its Chicago team. </p><p>Serhant is known for handling luxury listings, as well as marketing and selling new construction. Some of its active listings include a $185 million oceanfront estate in Palm Beach, Florida, and a $52 million newly built townhome in Manhattan.</p><p>The company's expansion comes as new brokerages — and mergers — rock the local real estate market. Last year, Baird & Warner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/06/27/local-real-estate-firms-baird-warner-dream-town-to-merge" >acquired</a> Dream Town, forming what was the second-largest brokerage in the region based on 2024 sales volume. And in December 2024, Chicago-based real estate brokerage @properties Christie’s International Real Estate was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/12/03/real-estate-giant-compass-acquires-chicago-properties-christies-444m-deal" >acquired by Compass</a>.</p><p>Serhant first expanded outside New York in 2023. It’s now active in 20 states, with locations in California, Colorado, Massachusetts and Texas opening this year, in addition to Illinois.</p>

entries.title: A look at what some former local hoops stars could have been worth in today's NIL college basketball world
entries.summary: <p>Name, image and likeness.</p><p>Dee Brown, the former Illinois basketball star, says he truly doesn’t think a whole lot about it — until he is regularly reminded by others.</p><p>“People always come up to me and mention something about it,” Brown said of today’s fans bringing up what he might have made in NIL as a college player. “But I stick to talking basketball and the different eras of the sport.”</p><p>The original intent of NIL — Name, Image and Likeness — made some sense.</p><p>NIL was simply put in place to be a personal branding opportunity for the college athlete. As a result, they would have the ability to profit off their identity. In a billion dollar college sports industry, NIL was put in place to recognize the value of the athlete, allowing them to be financially empowered.</p><p>But it went haywire quickly with no real guardrails or rules in place. As it became virtually unregulated, financial figures far surpassed anything anyone expected and rapidly turned into something it was not intended to: pay-for-play.</p><p>With compensation for athletes basically doubling every year since NIL arrived in 2021, the dollar amounts being thrown around in recent years has been pretty mind-boggling. We’re talking $1 million student-athletes who play roles off the bench.</p><p>“No doubt I’ve thought about it, because people bring it to my attention,” Brown admits. “But I will say this … I am happy and thankful that I played in the era that I did. I wouldn’t be the person I am today, and I wouldn’t have the genuine love for the game if I hadn’t played in the era that I did.</p><p>“I’m not saying the kids don’t have it now, but if I made that much money as a college kid? I’m not sure I would have had the same motivation and hunger that I did. I know myself. Plus, I think you kind of miss the chance to be a real college student.”</p><p>For some it wouldn’t have mattered a whole lot. Jalen Brunson is in the middle of a $156 million contract with the Knicks. Anthony Davis has made over $350 million in his career. So adding a few million more in their college days doesn’t move the needle a whole lot financially.</p><p>But for many others — we’re talking elite players who were game-changers at the college level — missing out on the college dough is a tougher pill to swallow, particularly for those not quite good enough to cash in NBA checks.</p><p>After hearing what college players in the transfer portal and top incoming freshmen received over the past several months, while also talking to many college basketball coaches for their takes, here are several individual scenarios of past Illinois prep greats.</p><p>Starting with the aforementioned Brown, who would have been the poster boy for all that NIL was intended to be for the student-athlete, here is how the plot may have played out at different points in the college careers of various well-known players.</p><h3>Dee Brown, Illinois (2005)</h3><p>The Illinois legend could have asked for the world in NIL compensation two decades ago. In theory, Brown was the quintessential Name, Image and Likeness student-athlete with his popularity, personality and marketability.</p><p>Fresh off an iconic Illinois basketball season, it was a perfect storm for Brown in the spring of 2005.</p><p>A senior-to-be, Brown had just helped lead the Fighting Illini to a 37-2 record and a national runner-up finish. Fellow star Deron Williams and leading scorer Luther Head were off to the NBA. Illinois would have had to do whatever it took to keep Brown, a preseason All-American who every program in the country would have coveted.</p><p>Also, on top of the straight pay-to-play compensation, this would have been the rare player who would have been richly rewarded and compensated for actual real endorsement deals.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following junior year: $5 million</b></p><h3>Cameron Krutwig, Loyola</h3><p>Flashback to the 2017-18 season. The big man was a central figure for a Cinderella Final Four team as a freshman, playing 23 minutes a game while averaging 10.5 points and 6.1 rebounds a game. Krutwig’s star was just beginning to rise.</p><p>Remember, this was a Loyola program playing in the Missouri Valley Conference at the time. With the limited resources in place, there would have been no way for coach Porter Moser to keep Krutwig in the fold for another year.</p><p>But Krutwig would have also been a different type of portal target, a niche big man, who would have had a few less suitors as his game wouldn’t have played ideally in, say, the SEC. Nonetheless, he’s finding a spot somewhere at the high-major level for a couple million.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following freshman year: $2.1 million</b></p><h3>Tyler Ulis, Kentucky</h3><p>This one could have dramatically changed the course for both Ulis and Kentucky, following the 2015-16 season.</p><p>As a sophomore in Lexington, Ulis turned in an All-American season. The former Marian Catholic superstar did it all as both the Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year in the SEC. He averaged 17.3 points and seven assists a game as the 5-9 floor general set the UK single-season assists record.</p><p>His stock was never going to be higher, especially for a player at his size, and he declared for the 2016 NBA Draft after just two college seasons. Phoenix took Ulis in the second round with the 34th pick. He played 133 career NBA games, making a little over $2 million.</p><p>A returning All-American at a crazed-Blue Blood like Kentucky? Even with his ceiling as high as it could possibly be, the temptation to return to Kentucky — and be really paid — would have been more than just tempting. In the end he played 133 career NBA games, making a little over $2 million in salary over two seasons. If he came back to Kentucky?</p><p>The college player returning for another season is the scenario we are seeing more and more today due to the NIL dollars.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following sophomore year: $3.5 million</b></p><h3>Jacob Pullen, Kansas State</h3><p>The dynamic scoring guard was a bit overlooked coming out of Proviso East. But he instantly made an impact, upping his scoring average from 9.7 points a game as a freshman to 13.9 as a sophomore.</p><p>Already at a high-major program, Pullen would have been compensated early in his career. But after putting up 19.3 points a game as a junior in 2009-10, Pullen could have entered the portal to gauge his value and set the market for his services as a senior.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following junior year: $2.8 million</b></p><h3>Bryan Mullins, Southern Illinois</h3><p>Mullins, the former Southern Illinois head coach and current DePaul assistant, would be a unique case study in this NIL-pay era.</p><p>Mullins didn’t put up whopping numbers. But following his sophomore season, his value would have still been extremely high as a winning point guard for a NCAA Tournament team that reached the Sweet 16.</p><p>With Mullins, a tough, savvy, defensive stalwart as a lead guard, it would have been all about a high-major program and the coaching staff valuing everything to do with winning. Even while averaging just 6.3 points a game as a sophomore in that 2016-07 season, his stock would have been high –– too high to stay in Carbondale for another season.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following his sophomore year: $750,000</b></p><h3>DJ Cooper, Ohio</h3><p>The former Seton Academy star immediately took the Mid-American Conference by storm. He averaged 13.5 points a game as a freshman while leading the league in assists with 5.9 per game — and helping Ohio to a NCAA Tournament upset win over Georgetown with 23 points.</p><p>Could Ohio have kept Cooper? Probably not. But let's say Ohio managed to keep the point guard for one more season. He again put up a league-leading 7.5 assists a game as a sophomore while upping his scoring to 15.8 points a game.</p><p>Cooper is certainly out the door and heading to a high-major for the next two seasons.</p><p>The possible domino effect would have been interesting? Ohio doesn’t go to the Sweet 16 during Cooper’s junior season at Ohio, and coach John Groce isn’t in position to take the Illinois job in the spring of 2012.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following sophomore year: $1.8 million</b></p><h3>John Shurna, Northwestern</h3><p>People forget the type of career and impact the former Glenbard West star had at Northwestern. He scored over 2,000 career points and is the second all-time leading scorer.</p><p>But would the Wildcats have been able to keep Shurna in the fold after he averaged 20 points and seven rebounds a game as a sophomore in the 2009-10 season? The education and degree does help.</p><p>Although Northwestern isn’t a program known to be swimming in NIL dollars, the Wildcats have done a nice job keeping their recent stars, namely Boo Buie and Nick Martinelli, out of the portal.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following sophomore year: $2.5 million</b></p><h3>Osiris Eldridge, Illinois State</h3><p>One of the real underrated players to come out of the city, the 6-3 guard was a star at Illinois State. He finished his career with 1,838 points while making 278 three-pointers. But the Redbirds would have not been able to keep him around for more than two years.</p><p>Eldridge averaged 9.5 points a game as a freshman for coach Porter Moser, who was fired at the conclusion of the 2006-07 season. With his coach fired, the belief was Eldridge might leave.</p><p>Newly-hired Tim Jankovich put together a coaching staff that included Paris Parham — Eldridge’s high school coach at Phillips — and the standout stayed and went on to explode as a sophomore. With production (15.8 points a game), efficiency (39 percent from three) and explosive athleticism to boot, keeping Eldridge any longer would have been impossible on a Missouri Valley Conference NIL budget.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following sophomore year: $1.8 million</b></p><h3>Jared Brownridge, Santa Clara</h3><p>Does anyone even realize the 6-2 sniper from Waubonsie Valley is the second all-time leading scorer in Santa Clara history with 2,313 points?</p><p>Remember, this is a program that has produced NBA players Steve Nash, Kurt Rambis and recent NBA star Jalen Williams.</p><p>Brownridge played all four seasons at Santa Clara. But he could have left the West Coast Conference school at any point and cashed in after putting up a whopping 20.5 points a game as a freshman. He also shot an incredible 43 percent from three that freshman season while making a ridiculous 95 three-pointers.</p><p>While Santa Clara does have some financial resources playing in the WCC, Brownridge would have had to test the waters at some point. And after that phenomenal freshman season in 2013-14? Someone would have blown the number past what Santa Clara could have likely afforded.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following freshman year: $2 million</b></p><h3>Keifer Sykes, Wisconsin-Green Bay</h3><p>The former Marshall star is a prime example of the type of career you’ll never see again in a conference like the Horizon League. The 5-11 point guard thrived immediately as a freshman, stayed all four years and scored over 2,000 career points.</p><p>Let’s just say coach Brian Wardle was able to keep his young star around for one more year following a freshman season where he averaged 11.2 points and 3.3 assists a game. The electric Sykes was certainly out the door after putting up 15.9 points and 4.3 assists a game as a sophomore.</p><p>High-major programs would have been courting Sykes in the spring of 2013.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following sophomore year: $850,000</b></p><h3>Patrick Miller, Tennessee State</h3><p>The strong, relentless guard from Hales Franciscan averaged an Ohio Valley Conference-best 23.7 points a game as a senior in 2013-14. In today’s college basketball world it would have never happened –– and those poor TSU fans would have missed out on one of the greatest individual seasons in program history.</p><p><b>Possible NIL value following junior year: $500,000</b></p><h3>DePaul’s recruiting Class of 1998 </h3><p>DePaul basketball was floundering in the late 1990s. Enter coach Pat Kennedy.</p><p>True story. As I was sitting with Kennedy at the old Morris Shootout in the summer of 1997, just a short time after he had been hired as DePaul’s new head coach, we engaged in a very open conversation on recruiting.</p><p>I asked him, “How are things on the recruiting front?”</p><p>The charismatic Kennedy responded with as much excitement and confidence as any coach could possibly have.</p><p>“Great. We are going to get him, him and him,” Kennedy answered as he pointed out three separate players in the Morris Fieldhouse that summer day. “And I also have this little point guard from out east we’re going to get who you’re going to love.”</p><p>The players? Quentin Richardson, Lance Williams and Bobby Simmons –– three city stars ranked No. 9, No. 24 and No. 26, respectively, in the country — and mighty mite Rashon Burno, who played for Bob Hurley, Sr., at St. Anthony’s in Jersey City before a year of prep school.</p><p>But how much would that freshman class have cost in today’s dollars?</p><p>For where DePaul was as a program at that time — the Blue Demons were 3-23 in the 1996-97 season — an overpay would have been necessary to keep the local stars home and out of reach of Blue Bloods and Big Ten powers. The numbers would be staggering for the average fan to see as it would cost DePaul right around $5 million for the four freshmen.</p><p><b>Possible NIL values following sophomore year: Quentin Richardson ($2.2 million); Lance Williams ($1.5 million); Bobby Simmons ($1.2 million); Rashon Burno ($450,000).</b></p>

entries.title: New coach Matt Majkrzak looks to change NIU's basketball fortunes
entries.summary: <p>There is a fresh, new beginning at Northern Illinois.</p><p>The clean slate a brand new coaching staff offers can overshadow what NIU basketball has proven over the past several decades: It’s a very difficult basketball coaching job.</p><p>The difficulty, however, is likely why first-year coach Matt Majkrzak was hired last March –– at least he thinks so.</p><p>“It’s probably why I got the job, because they wanted to know what needed to be different,” Majkrzak said.</p><p>And Majkrzak believes that finding success at a place that hasn’t had it in quite some fits him perfectly.</p><p>“You almost need someone who is used to being at a hard job,” said Majkrzak, who spent the previous seven years as the head coach at Division II Northern Michigan. “Northern Michigan was bad, so it’s not like a new thing in trying to turn around something.”</p><p>Majkrzak went 136-73 at Northern Michigan. He guided the Wildcats to the last four Division II NCAA Tournaments while averaging 24 wins a year. Prior to Majkrzak, NMU went two decades without a 20-win season and posted single-digit win totals in eight of the previous 12 seasons.</p><p>Majkrzak believes when you have a coach coming from a higher level — the previous six NIU coaching hires came from the high-major ranks of college basketball — it’s easier to get caught up in all the things you don’t have or are limited by.</p><p>“I think that is definitely a different approach from our end, because we look at things and can’t believe all the things we do have in comparison to Division II,” Majkrzak points out.”</p><p>But Northern Illinois basketball has been another degree of difficulty.</p><p>History, particularly recent history, is proof of the assessment of how difficult a job it is in DeKalb.</p><p>Since NIU joined the Mid-American Conference in 1997, the basketball program has won 20 or more games one single time. That was a 21-13 season in 2015-16. And in those 29 years in the MAC, the Huskies put together a winning conference record only three times.</p><p>That three-decade track record covers — or has taken down — five different head coaches. The last coach to leave Northern Illinois still standing was Jim Molinari way back in 1991. He guided the Huskies to a 25-win season and NCAA Tournament before departing for Bradley.</p><p>For an abundance of reasons not meant for this story, the program has faced several issues in getting it turned around.</p><p>But a fresh start with a coaching change will always provide hope. And that’s where Director of Athletics Sean Frazier is at after an out-of-the-box hire in Majkrzak.</p><p>But coaching is coaching and winning is winning no matter the level. And while every first-year coach believes they will win when taking over a new program, Majkrzak has experienced and tasted it.</p><p>NIU basketball also makes the move next year to the Horizon League. That’s a plus in that the league is a step down from banging heads with the likes of Akron, Toledo, Kent State and Miami-Ohio in the MAC, basketball programs with far greater resources for basketball than NIU.</p><p>“I really like the idea of places and jobs in basketball where you can be really successful but haven’t been,” Majkrzak said. “There isn’t as much pressure to do it a certain way. You have the freedom to build the program exactly how you want. You aren’t trying to replicate what someone did two years ago or five years ago. I thought specifically at NIU you have a chance to do that.”</p>

entries.title: Cook County pledges $8 million to help south suburban communities clean summer storm damage
entries.summary: <p>Cook County pledged $8 million to help south suburban communities clean up from severe storms over the summer.</p><p>"This $8 million investment is about making sure our municipalities have the resources and the capacity to recover from this disaster," Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle told reporters at a press conference in Oak Forest Tuesday morning. "This is not about moving debris alone. It's also about helping municipalities restore their communities and move forward."</p><p>Preckwinkle noted the county has helped remove roughly 100,000 cubic yards of debris — enough to fill about 5,700 dump trucks. </p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/11/severe-weather-expected-in-chicago-area-and-other-areas-of-illinois" target="_blank" >Aug. 11 storms</a> produced tornadoes that left a half-million customers without power in the Chicago area, as tree limbs and downed power lines were scattered throughout the southern suburbs. </p><p>"Our commitment to the residents of Cook County does not end when the storm passes," Preckwinkle said. "We'll continue until the work of recovery is done."</p>
