entries.title: IHSA football playoff qualifiers with two wins? That should be enough for several teams
entries.summary: <p>With just two weeks remaining in the regular season, attention is quickly turning to the state playoffs.</p><p>The Illinois High School Association has entered a new era, expanding the state playoffs to 384 teams. Each of the eight classes now has 48 teams, up from the traditional 32. It is the first playoff expansion since 1985.</p><p>The top 16 seeds in each class will receive a bye in the Opening Round. That’s what the IHSA is calling the new first round: the Opening Round. And it appears the second round will be called the First Round. That’s silly, but that is how the IHSA currently lists the tournament on its website: Opening Round, First Round, Second Round, Quarterfinals, Semifinals, Championship.</p><p>Shaw Media’s Steve Soucie spends the season <a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/friday-night-drive/2026/09/30/ihsa-football-playoff-projections-new-system-changes-games-in-focus-for-final-weeks/" target="_blank" >prognosticating the state playoff bracket</a>. According to Soucie, every three-win football team will make the expanded state playoffs.</p><p>The Public League’s unknown Week 9 schedule adds some uncertainty to Soucie’s work, but as of last week, Soucie expected 20 two-win teams to qualify for the playoffs.</p><p>There are currently 33 two-win teams in the area. They all have two more chances to win one game, get that third win, and guarantee a playoff spot.</p><p>Here are a few of the biggest names still vying for a third win and a playoff guarantee.</p><p><b>Benet:</b> New coach James White was a splashy hire for the school. But the Redwings dropped winnable games against Marmion and Notre Dame and now face an uphill battle. They are at St. Rita in Week 8 and host St. Patrick in Week 9. Three wins appear unlikely unless Benet pulls off an upset…but Soucie’s projections have the Redwings sneaking in as a No. 46 seed with just two wins.</p><p><b>Carmel:</b> Another team coached by a former NFL player (Jason McKie), the Corsairs actually opened the season in the Super 25. They are a talented team that hasn’t played poorly. But the schedule has been brutal. Carmel lost to Hersey, Providence, Montini, St. Ignatius and Marist. Expect the Corsairs to beat De La Salle on Friday and grab their third win to qualify for the playoffs.</p><p><b>Glenbrook North:</b> The Spartans are in a similar situation to Carmel, facing a winless Maine East in Week 8. Expect Glenbrook North to pick up its third win on Friday.</p><p><b>St. Laurence:</b> Few teams in the area have been as successful in the playoffs over the past few seasons as the Vikings. But they have a tough final two games, hosting Marist in Week 8 and visiting DePaul Prep in Week 9. St. Laurence’s strength of schedule will likely help it grab a playoff spot as a two-win team.</p><p><b>Simeon:</b> Many of Sinque Turner’s key players are sophomores and would benefit greatly by gaining state playoff experience this season. The Wolverines face Taft (3-4) this week and are favored. Their Week 9 opponent is still TBD. But there is good news for Simeon. Soucie’s projection has the Wolverines making the 6A field with just two wins.</p><p>Clearly, it is a new world. All five teams mentioned above could sneak into the playoffs with just two wins. According to Soucie’s projection, to be released in a few days, only three of the 24 Catholic League teams are on pace to miss the playoffs: De La Salle (0-7), Marian Catholic (2-5) and St. Viator (1-6).</p>

entries.title: Chicago cop fired 2 guns during off-duty shooting that left person wounded in Little Village
entries.summary: <p>An off-duty Chicago police officer shot a person while firing two guns during an argument this weekend in Little Village, the Civilian Office for Police Accountability announced Tuesday. </p><p>The officer was driving in the 2600 block of West 24th Street and encountered a group of people around 12:45 a.m. Sunday, according to statements from COPA and the Chicago Police Department. The officer exchanged words with a male in the group, then fired a gun "multiple times," officials said.</p><p>The officer then drove toward the 2300 block of South Rockwell Street, got out of his vehicle and "fired additional shots from two firearms simultaneously" toward the area of the initial altercation, COPA said. A male was shot twice and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in fair condition, police said. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/04/off-duty-cpd-officer-shooting-little-village-two-injured" >Police initially described the male as an “offender”</a> and said he had struck the cop in the face during the argument. COPA didn't subsequently report that detail.</p><p>The male was taken into custody after the shooting, but he was later released without charges, police said. Police spokespeople haven't provided his age and couldn't immediately say whether he remained hospitalized.</p><p>A second male suffered an injury to his arm and took himself to Mount Sinai in good condition, police said, without noting how he was injured.</p><p>The officer was treated for minor injuries and released from the hospital, COPA said. He was placed on administrative duties amid the COPA investigation.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/04/off-duty-cpd-officer-shooting-little-village-two-injured" target="_blank" >Off-duty CPD officer shoots man during argument in Little Village</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bulls' Matas Buzelis having his patience tested and hopes to be passing
entries.summary: <p>This is not where Matas Buzelis wanted to be in Year 3 of his NBA career.</p><p>It’s not where he wanted to be as a rookie, and it was obviously not where he wanted to be last season, evident by his body language at times late in the year.</p><p>In a Bulls jersey? He loves that.</p><p>In the basement of the standings since getting selected No. 11 overall in the 2024 draft? No, and it hasn’t been sitting well.</p><p>That’s why the day before the preseason tips off for the Bulls on Wednesday was a good time for a wellness check on the forward.</p><p>“Yeah, one thing, just practicing patience,” Buzelis said, being reminded of all of his focus on winning when he first joined the franchise a few years back. “Everything can’t come to you at once.”</p><p>Asked if that’s been difficult for him, Buzelis replied, “It was hard for me. But I speak to a lot of people. A lot of smart, intelligent people, and they tell me everything comes with time. This team is capable of a lot of things, and I know we’ll get to where we want to get to. It’s a process, but all of us are working extremely hard to try and achieve our goals.”</p><p>A much different tone than late in the 2025-26 campaign, especially in the wake of a roster purge at the trade deadline and then uncertainty hovering over the old front office and coaching staff. Buzelis sounded down after games, searching for some sort of glimmer of hope.</p><p>“It was hard for me,” Buzelis admitted. “Last year was hard. Sometimes you’ve got to go through stuff in your life to notice that you want better. Last year was very hard. There was no type of rhythm. We didn’t know who was playing, we didn’t know how we were going to play. Now, there’s more structure, everyone is in a role, and you know what you’re going to get every night.</p><p>“You gotta go through stuff and that builds you as a person.”</p><p>All well and good but the Bulls can go through a season of positive vibes and still realistically finish in the same standings neighborhood as they have the previous few years.</p><p>The new front office has stressed patience and called this a “rebuild,” which would seemingly contradict what Buzelis has demanded from himself since joining the organization.</p><p>That’s for people above his pay grade to worry about as far as Buzelis was concerned.</p><p>“We have a special group,” he said. “It will take time, but I don’t focus on the long term. We have a game (against the Suns on Wednesday) and we’re looking to win.”</p><p>So has Buzelis had to change his mentality a bit? Maybe. But he’s also 21 years old now and not a wide-eyed 18-year-old. The front office led by executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham and new coach in Tiago Splitter have made that process easier for him.</p><p>There’s also a way different roster structure. Last year at this time, then-executive Arturas Karnisovas thought it would be just fine to start the season with eight lame-duck players dealing with expiring contracts and trade rumors.</p><p>Graham does have moveable pieces if he wants to play that game, but they are all veteran players that understand the business of basketball.</p><p>“There’s more structure (this season), but I would say the drills we do, everything is more focused, more intense, so that’s where I mix in that word structure,” Buzelis said. “It’s a little more strict. It’s also new faces, everyone wants to show up, everyone wants to compete, and that’s kind of where I was headed (with the strict comment).”</p>

entries.title: Mujer de Chicago baleada por la Patrulla Fronteriza demanda al gobierno federal, presenta pruebas contra agente
entries.summary: <p>El ex fiscal federal que ahora busca que Marimar Martínez obtenga justicia dijo el lunes que su equipo legal reunió suficientes pruebas para presentar cargos penales contra el agente de inmigración que le disparó el otoño pasado durante el Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>Christopher Parente hizo esa afirmación al anunciar la muy esperada demanda de Martínez contra el gobierno federal. <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/3e/79/71b60db147428d8edf68a2e6e2c5/martinezvusa.pdf" target="_blank" >Ella demandó</a> por el tiroteo del 4 de octubre de 2025 a manos del agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Charles Exum, y por el fallido intento posterior de las autoridades federales de procesarla.</p><p>Para sustentar la demanda, los abogados de Martínez contrataron a expertos que elaboraron una reconstrucción forense del tiroteo. La presentación busca mostrar cómo Exum disparó cada uno de sus cinco tiros contra la camioneta Nissan Rogue de Martínez, incluido un último disparo que presuntamente atravesó la ventana trasera del lado del pasajero.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-270000" name="module-270000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Parente y el abogado Michael Gallagher dijeron a los periodistas que planeaban compartir la presentación con las autoridades. En el camino, invocaron la etiqueta que el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) le aplicó a Martínez el otoño pasado y preguntaron: “¿Quién es realmente el terrorista doméstico?”</p><p>“Alguien tiene que hacer algo”, dijo Parente, quien alguna vez trabajó como fiscal federal en Chicago y Miami.</p><p>El tono duro es típico de los abogados que presentan demandas. Pero lo dicho el lunes ocurrió en medio de un esfuerzo continuo por responsabilizar a los agentes por su conducta durante Midway Blitz. La agresiva campaña de deportaciones que sembró caos en las calles de la ciudad provocó varias demandas, incluida una presentada por Illinois y Chicago contra DHS.</p><p>Pero ningún agente federal ha sido acusado de un delito cometido en servicio relacionado con Midway Blitz.</p><p>La Policía de Chicago sí ha comenzado a investigar el tiroteo contra Martínez. La investigación ha sido asignada a una unidad integrada por detectives con experiencia, que buscarán llevar un caso ante los fiscales del Condado Cook, informó el Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>La oficina de la Fiscal estatal del Condado Cook, Eileen O’Neill Burke, dijo que las fuerzas del orden tienen que construir un caso antes de que su equipo pueda considerar cargos. Burke dijo apenas el mes pasado que ninguna agencia les había presentado un caso así contra un agente federal.</p><p>El Departamento de Justicia se negó a comentar el lunes. DHS repitió la versión anterior de que Exum había sido descansado, sin ofrecer detalles adicionales.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-058eb7" name="image-058eb7"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9b32dd5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3a%2Fa8%2Fc5ec013a4f1dacae17590b561cc2%2Fmartinez-260202-067.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/630515d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3a%2Fa8%2Fc5ec013a4f1dacae17590b561cc2%2Fmartinez-260202-067.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4b7e8cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3a%2Fa8%2Fc5ec013a4f1dacae17590b561cc2%2Fmartinez-260202-067.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Marimar Martínez muestra una de las cicatrices de sus heridas de bala durante una entrevista en los estudios de grabación de Chicago Public Media en Navy Pier, el domingo 1 de febrero de 2026. Martínez sobrevivió a cinco disparos de un agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza en Chicago el otoño pasado. | Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4b7e8cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3a%2Fa8%2Fc5ec013a4f1dacae17590b561cc2%2Fmartinez-260202-067.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/382501e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3a%2Fa8%2Fc5ec013a4f1dacae17590b561cc2%2Fmartinez-260202-067.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4b7e8cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3a%2Fa8%2Fc5ec013a4f1dacae17590b561cc2%2Fmartinez-260202-067.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Marimar Martínez muestra una de las cicatrices de sus heridas de bala durante una entrevista en los estudios de grabación de Chicago Public Media en Navy Pier, el domingo 1 de febrero de 2026. Martínez sobrevivió a cinco disparos de un agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza en Chicago el otoño pasado.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Exum le disparó a Martínez cinco veces después de que ella lo vio conducir una camioneta Chevrolet Tahoe que también llevaba a otros dos agentes y comenzó a seguirlos en su Rogue. Ella tocó la bocina de su vehículo, gritó “la migra” y trató de advertirle a la gente sobre los agentes.</p><p>Luego, cerca de la calle 39th y la Avenida Kedzie, dijo que Exum se desvió hacia su Rogue y que ambos vehículos se rozaron. Las imágenes de la cámara corporal parecían mostrar a Exum girando el volante hacia la izquierda, hacia la Rogue de Martínez, justo antes del choque.</p><p>Aunque Martínez primero detuvo su Rogue, dijo que temía ser agredida por los agentes. Por eso, dijo, se desvió hacia su extrema izquierda para evitarlos mientras ellos se bajaban de su vehículo, y así poder huir.</p><p>Exum abrió fuego, le disparó a Martínez y le causó siete heridas. Más tarde, la oficina del fiscal federal de Estados Unidos Andrew Boutros en Chicago la acusó de agredir a un agente federal, pero desestimó el caso casi dos meses después.</p><p>Mientras tanto, el entonces comandante de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Gregory Bovino, ofreció, después del tiroteo, posponer la jubilación de Exum tras su “excelente servicio en Chicago”, según los registros.</p><p>Ahora Martínez presentó su demanda contra el gobierno de Estados Unidos, en la que alega negligencia, lesiones intencionales, agresión, imposición intencional de angustia emocional, procesamiento malicioso, detención arbitraria y encarcelamiento ilegal.</p><p>Gallagher y Parente dijeron que es poco probable llegar a un acuerdo. “Esto es un juicio”, dijo Gallagher.</p><p>Martínez, ciudadana estadounidense nacida y criada en Chicago, comenzó a criticar de forma destacada la campaña de deportaciones del gobierno de Trump a inicios de este año, después de que las autoridades migratorias en Minneapolis mataran a tiros a Renee Good y Alex Pretti.</p><p>“Yo soy su voz”, dijo Martínez al Sun-Times en febrero. “Estoy aquí por una razón”.</p><p>La reconstrucción de la escena del tiroteo, realizada por Jeremy Bauer, de Bauer Forensics LLC, debilita aún más la afirmación original del gobierno federal de que Martínez y otro hombre “embistieron” a los agentes con sus vehículos y que Martínez condujo su vehículo hacia Exum, dijeron sus abogados.</p><p>También contradice la presunta declaración anterior de Exum al FBI, en la que afirmó que dejó de disparar una vez que ya no estaba en la trayectoria del vehículo de Martínez, dijeron sus abogados.</p><p>Bauer utilizó una inspección del vehículo de Martínez, sus heridas y fotos y videos de la escena del tiroteo para reconstruir lo ocurrido, dijo Gallagher.</p><p>Parente dijo que Exum ni siquiera estaba en la trayectoria de la Rogue cuando disparó sus primeros tres tiros al parabrisas desde el lado del pasajero del vehículo. El cuarto pasó por la ventana delantera del pasajero, dijo Parente. El quinto, añadió, atravesó la ventana trasera del lado del pasajero.</p><p>“Él está detrás del vehículo, disparándole”, dijo Parente.</p><p>La demanda de Martínez incluso alega que “el agente Exum caminaba hacia el vehículo de Marimar mientras seguía disparando su arma”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Una imagen de una reconstrucción del tiroteo de Marimar Martínez en octubre de 2025 por parte del agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza Charles Exum.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>La <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ilac/documents/final-report/IAC-Final-Report-April-2026.pdf" target="_blank" >Comisión de Responsabilidad de Illinois</a> concluyó en abril que Exum “le disparó sin justificación aparente a una civil desarmada”; que “se manipularon y destruyeron pruebas de forma deliberada”; y que “agentes federales elaboraron informes oficiales materialmente inexactos”.</p><p>Martínez sí llevaba un arma de fuego ese día, pero estaba dentro de una funda color de rosa brillante en el fondo de su bolso, y la funda estaba cerrada, según muestran registros judiciales.</p><p>El gobernador JB Pritzker, quien creó la comisión, escribió en redes sociales el fin de semana pasado que Martínez “merece verdadera justicia y rendición de cuentas por parte del gobierno federal”.</p><p>Existen vías para que fiscales estatales presenten cargos penales contra agentes federales bajo ciertas circunstancias. La pregunta legal clave es si los agentes federales actuaron de manera razonable al cumplir con sus funciones.</p><p>O’Neill Burke le dijo a WBEZ el mes pasado sobre otro posible obstáculo al que podría enfrentarse: dijo que la fuerza pública federal no está sujeta a citaciones de cortes estatales. Y si los fiscales no tienen en sus manos la evidencia adecuada, añadió, eso posiblemente “haría que el caso estuviera sujeto a desestimación”.</p><p>Pero los abogados de Martínez recibieron un gran volumen de esa evidencia después de que el gobierno intentó procesarla el otoño pasado, señala la demanda. Incluía imágenes de cámaras corporales, mensajes de texto de Exum y declaraciones grabadas de los agentes al FBI y a los fiscales federales.</p><p>Las autoridades federales presentaron cargos contra al menos 33 personas conocidas, incluida Martínez, en relación con Midway Blitz. La mayoría de esos casos se vinieron abajo sin llegar a una condena.</p><p>Parente señaló el lunes esas fallidas persecuciones, muchas de ellas relacionadas con el Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE), al argumentar a favor de cargos contra Exum.</p><p>“Si algún manifestante se acercaba demasiado a un agente de ICE, estornudaba sobre un agente de ICE, tosía sobre un agente de ICE, hablaba alrededor de agentes de ICE, lo acusaban con cargos de conspiración; lo acusaban de agresión. Lo acusaban de lesiones, de inmediato, por este Departamento de Justicia, sin ninguna investigación”.</p><p>En cuanto al tiroteo de Martínez, dijo, “no ha habido investigación. No ha habido cargos”.</p><p>Pero, agregó Parente, “creemos que hemos reunido pruebas concluyentes para acusar a Charles Exum de cargos penales aquí en Illinois.</p><p>“Ya sea a través del sistema federal o del sistema estatal”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Bears own Packers now, right? Ben Johnson over Matt LaFleur, right? Is it Sunday yet? What could go wrong?
entries.summary: <p>Three things I think I know about the 3-1 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, who might not be able to win a game with a sack of potatoes under center but have to like where they are heading into a Week 5 visit to Green Bay:</p><p><b>1. They absolutely, positively own the Packers: </b>After all, the Bears have beaten their bitter rivals — hang on while I dig through the files — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/12/20/bears-packers-qb-jordan-love-leaves-saturday-nfl-game-after-being-hit-in-head" target="_blank" >twice in a row</a>. So what if the Packers won 11 straight in the series from 2019 to 2024? Not to mention the Packers’ 15-2 stretch, including the 2010 NFC Championship Game, right before that. Or pretty much three whole decades starting with the mid-1990s. Call it a 30-year blip.</p><p>On second thought, let’s put the “own” on hold. But it’s undeniable the Bears (plus-47 in points) have been much better than the 2-2 Packers (minus-32) so far. The Bears also are healthier even factoring in Caleb Williams’ hamstring injury, which will keep the quarterback out of action for a third straight game as Tyson Bagent gets his second start. It’s wild to see a Bears team favored (by 2½ points) in a game at Lambeau Field, but here we are.</p><p><b>2. Ben Johnson has it better than Matt LaFleur: </b>The Bears’ coach can do no wrong. He mildly disses his Packers counterpart with a blow-by handshake after a game, and all is fine. He F-bombs and says he “hates” the Packers in the locker room after a game, and Bears fans want to write him in for governor. He’s intense and can be prickly, but he’s off to a 14-7 start and celebrated for it at every turn.</p><p>Then there’s LaFleur, who’s 78-42-1 — an elite record — and 12-3 against the Bears and, naturally, taking shots from all sides. Even former Packers QB Kurt Benkert, who will post on social media 47 more times before you reach the end of this sentence, ripped LaFleur last week as lacking confidence and being rather humorless. This must be what happens when you suddenly can’t run the ball, can’t avoid drops in the passing game and have a knack for blowing big leads.</p><p>LaFleur is keeping it classy in regard to the Bears, at least.</p><p>“I mean, they’re the defending [NFC] North champions,” he said. “So what a great opportunity and great challenge for us in our home stadium to play against the defending champs.”</p><p><b>3. D’Andre Swift better stop fumbling: </b>The No. 1 running back has put the ball on the ground twice this season, right around the average for his NFL career. A one-man epidemic? Hardly, but Johnson didn’t sound like a coach with any patience for it when discussing it this week.</p><p>As well as Kyle Monangai — who last fumbled in a game in high school — is running it, we could see him in heavier doses for a while. Another 30-carry game like the one he had against the Jets isn’t like to happen, but right now he’s the hot hand. Monangai handled the ball 700-plus times at Rutgers without fumbling and is almost at 1,000 factoring in his Bears touches. How did he last until the seventh round again?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7b0000" name="image-7b0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/aec8505/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2Fc1%2F7f489fa74f209da2634c1d62c478%2Fap26242747819302.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5442143/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2Fc1%2F7f489fa74f209da2634c1d62c478%2Fap26242747819302.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4b6761/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2Fc1%2F7f489fa74f209da2634c1d62c478%2Fap26242747819302.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Bears head coach Ben Johnson looks on during a preseason football game against the Tennessee Titans in Nashville on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4b6761/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2Fc1%2F7f489fa74f209da2634c1d62c478%2Fap26242747819302.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cab7ee9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2Fc1%2F7f489fa74f209da2634c1d62c478%2Fap26242747819302.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4b6761/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2Fc1%2F7f489fa74f209da2634c1d62c478%2Fap26242747819302.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Bears head coach Ben Johnson looks on during a preseason football game against the Tennessee Titans in Nashville on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Stew Milne/AP </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Ben-o-meter: 9 out of 10</b></h3><p>Wins with three different QBs in the first four games of the season have Johnson among the top three in coach of the year odds on leading betting sites. Yes, already. No kidding, it’s way early.</p><p>Besides, a Packers game is the real barometer.</p><h3><b>Take the North</b></h3><p>Would you rather be in the Bears shoes or in those of the 2-2 Lions, who rank last in the NFL in pass defense and total defense? Things can change fast, but at present it’s an easy answer.</p><p>Same goes for the Bears relative to the Packers, who have the bottom-ranked rushing attack (Bears rank No. 1) and don’t even have a rushing touchdown yet (Bears have nine). But the Bears are 9-28 in the division since 2019, a stat that makes one suspect the wheels could still come off at any time.</p><p>The winning-ugly Vikings remain in the best spot at 4-0 after a 15-10 win against the putrid Dolphins.</p><h3><b>Three and Out</b></h3><p><b>1. Turnover magic: </b>So far, the Bears don’t have it. After topping the NFL in both takeaways and fewest turnovers committed last season — their plus-22 turnover margin was the stat of the season, without a doubt — they’re a ho-hum plus-1 through four games. But when you’re doubling your opponents in third-down conversation rate (47.4% to 23.7%) and outpacing them by cartoonish margins in first downs (101 to 56) and time of possession (36:35 to 23:24), it’s sort of the same thing.</p><p><b>2. “Green Bay sucks!” </b>Lately, you can’t go anywhere without hearing this chant. Bears games against teams other than the Packers. White Sox playoff games. White Sox-Cubs crosstown matchups. Children’s birthday parties. Nunneries. Has the rivalry actually ramped up a level?</p><p><b>3. Time is a cruel mistress: </b>Wednesday marks 42 years since Walter Payton took a pitch from Jim McMahon and rumbled six yards to break the NFL’s career rushing record. Did the world exist in black-and-white then? It’s hard to remember.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/05/bears-packers-running-back-kyle-monangai-thumb-injury-not-considered-serious-micah-parsons-edgerrin-cooper-ben-johnson-matt-lafleur-nfl" target="_blank" >Bears report: RB Kyle Monangai’s thumb injury not considered serious</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/05/bears-packers-rivalry-ben-johnson-matt-lafleur-sunday-chance-back-up-words-lambeau-field-nfl" >Bears-Packers: Sunday is coach Ben Johnson’s chance to back up what he screamed in January</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/04/chicago-bears-defense-jets-ben-johnson-tyson-bagent-kyle-monangai-dillon-thieneman-geno-smith-isaiah-williams" >Bears’ defense — the No-Names of the Midway? — is standing up and demanding to be noticed</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Trump hasn’t redefined morality — he’s just worn some of us out
entries.summary: <p>Headlines are an odd art. You must summarize the story in a few words — in print, that is. With search engine optimization, online headlines tend to be these long, triple deck affairs redolent of an elaborate, almost Victorian complexity. Where once "Asteroid to hit earth?" would suffice, now we see, "Hurtling space asteroid on possible collision course, could destroy earth and all life upon it, including Taylor Swift."</p><p>Otherwise, brevity is still valued. Wit too. The Sun-Times is famous for both, often in the same headline: "DA POPE!" comes to mind, celebrating the joyful Chicago roots of the current vicar of Christ.</p><p>Long or short, the goal of any headline is to draw readers into a story. Plus accurately reflect both the story and reality. An article on Holocaust deniers should not be headlined, "Holocaust a hoax."</p><p>Though sometimes, fidelity to truth gets lost.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-5b0000" name="module-5b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Such as the headline on page A5 of The New York Times Monday: "Trump Has Moved the Boundaries of What Is Ethical."</p><p>He <i>has</i>?! That <i>is</i> news. Because while the president's second term has been noteworthy for ramping up the deceit, self-dealing, corruption and institution-shredding of his first administration, I have not gotten the memo that these things are now acceptable.</p><p>The article, by Peter Baker, the Times' veteran chief White House correspondent, begins by recounting how, seven years ago, when Trump tried to host the G7 summit at his own golf club, Trump National Doral Miami, "It incited an uproar among fellow Republicans, forcing him to scrap the idea."</p><p>No such trouble in 2026. Now his club is hosting the summit with "practically no protest." Which is true. The Republicans, whether active co-conspirators, or dazed hostages agreeing with their captor's every demand, are docile as sheep, with only the occasional soft bleat of anything that could, perhaps, be considered dissent.</p><p>Leading to the third paragraph, where we encounter what could be either another glaring untruth, or merely the kind of tone-deaf clunk that The New York Times is famous for, at least to this subscriber:</p><p>"The unprecedented blitz of self-enrichment by Mr. Trump," — the Times still uses honorifics, which is so cute, so old-school — "his family and his friends since he returned to the White House last year has become so extensive, so profligate and so brazen that he has effectively moved the goal posts of what is considered out of bounds."</p><p>Has he now? Moved those goalposts to the 30 yard line, where he scores lucrative goal after goal? I consider the president accepting gifts, whether bricks of gold from ambassadors, or luxury jets from oil sheikhs, to still be out of bounds. I consider Trump using the government to enrich himself to the tune of, to use Baker's figure, $2.2 billion and counting, to be completely unacceptable. As is his using taxpayer money to run commercials lauding himself. As is flouting the law by plastering his face on United States coins. As is making the government an artificial intelligence fanboy — whoops, he prefers "super intelligence fanboy" — to truckle his tech bro backers.</p><p>And on and on. And on. And on and on and on and on. Plus, you know, more.</p><p>To be fair, Baker catalogs what one watchdog calls "so much unprecedented and harmful corruption that it can be hard for the public to keep up with every story." Baker can't be faulted there. It's the "so now it's OK" tone that rattled me. It is not OK. It will never be OK.</p><p>Perhaps it is a matter of brevity. Maybe the original headline was "Trump Has Moved the Boundaries of What Is Ethical Among Co-Conspirators, Paid Lackeys, the Willfully Blind, and Cosseted East Coast Journalists Too Close to the Story to See the Forest from the Trees" but those last two dozen words were cut off in the editing process.</p><p>Here in the Midwest, however, breathing the free air of deep blue Illinois, we know the score. And we know what America stands for — the rule of law. Leaders who feel a responsibility to their constituents, whether a school district or an entire nation. Who try to do their jobs for the betterment of those constituents, for the people, and not line their pockets and turn the government into one vast chorus of self-praise. It's wrong. It was wrong last year and the year before and the year before that.</p><p>However long this nadir of American history lasts — whether it begins to end next month or just keeps digging deeper — moral values have not changed. What has happened is, they have been abused and ignored so successfully for so long that some people apparently have forgotten what they are, or can't imagine their return. I can.</p>

entries.title: Video gambling saturates Chicago area — here’s how many allow it, how many don’t
entries.summary: <p>Not even 20 years ago, video gambling was illegal in the Chicago region and the rest of Illinois.</p><p>Today, nearly 80% of the six-county metropolitan area has legalized video gambling, a level of saturation that means more than 200 municipalities now allow it to varying degrees, while more than 60 communities ban the machines, according to a Chicago Sun-Times examination that also found:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-863b5ba2-bc3d-11f1-a70e-f35c7d6bc731"><li>Wealthy suburbs generally outlaw video gambling — with the North Shore communities of Evanston, Glencoe, Highland Park, Highwood, Kenilworth, Lake Bluff, Lake Forest, Wilmette and Winnetka all with prohibitions — while lower-income south suburbs generally allow it, including Dixmoor and Ford Heights.<br></li><li>Some communities are rethinking their policies. North Chicago is tightening restrictions to “reduce the amount of gaming in town,” an official says. Bolingbrook recently scrapped a ban, legalizing video slots following a referendum. In Winfield, an advisory referendum is planned in the spring to gauge public support for keeping or lifting a ban.<br></li><li>Virtually every town in Kane, McHenry and Will counties now allows video gambling, while most of the municipal bans are concentrated in Cook, DuPage and Lake counties. The highest concentration of prohibitions are in DuPage and Lake, where nearly 40% of communities outlaw video gambling.<br></li><li>Many municipalities with casinos also allow video gambling elsewhere in town, including Elgin, Joliet and Waukegan but not Des Plaines. Next door in Rosemont, which wasn’t allowed to host a casino two decades ago because of concerns by regulators of reputed mob influence, there is a small amount of video gambling.<br></li><li>Some communities allow so-called “gaming cafes,” which are akin to mini-casinos, while others prohibit or restrict establishments where gambling is the main draw and revenue source over, for example, food and drinks. For some suburbs, it’s a moot point, as there are no establishments in town where video gambling could exist.</li></ul><p>There’s “no video gambling in Wayne,” said Patti Engstrom, the village clerk in the far west suburb. “We have no public gathering areas, no gas stations, no mini marts, no bars, no restaurants, no commercial whatsoever. We are an equestrian community. We have horses, not commercial businesses.”</p><p>For many years, video gambling devices were allowed in Chicago-area establishments only if they were used for “amusement” purposes and didn’t pay winnings — though many illicitly did in concert with the mob that controlled much of that underground industry.</p><p>An Illinois law legalizing video gambling terminals, or VGTs, was enacted in 2009, and the machines went live for “patron play” in September 2012.</p><p>“At the end of 2012, Illinois had 2,290 terminals generating $12.3 million in revenue,” according to a report from the Illinois Municipal League, which represents local governments.</p><p>“By 2025, the state had more than 49,000 terminals producing $3.19 billion in net terminal income revenue, resulting in nearly $1.12 billion in tax revenue, including $160 million distributed to municipalities and counties, and significant profits for video gaming establishments and terminal operators.”</p><p>The Illinois Gaming Board reports as of early September, “there are 8,799 video gaming locations and 50,049 VGTs and Illinois remains the largest regulated, distributed video gaming network of its kind in the world.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-740000" name="html-embed-module-740000"></a><div style="min-height:790px" id="datawrapper-vis-QHkjY"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/QHkjY/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-QHkjY"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/QHkjY/full.png" alt="A map of the collar counties of northeast Illinois, with several small dots placed throughout, all of the same size. Each dot represents a municipality (town or city or village) and is colored according to whether it allows video gambling terminals. The vast majority of dots are green, representing that they do allow the devices. Most of those that do not are clustered in the northern suburbs of Chicago, on either side of the border of Cook County and Lake County, especially toward the lake." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Ramifications of video gambling saturation</h3><p>Regulating gambling statewide, the government agency reports to Gov. JB Pritzker, who declined to say whether he believes video gambling has become too ubiquitous in Illinois — and brings about too many negative impacts.</p><p>Beyond gambling addiction, the vastness of video gambling also has the potential to normalize gambling for children, who are exposed to marketing. Studies show many who gamble are those who can least afford it. And video gambling is fueling a crime wave of after-hour burglaries at establishments with the machines.</p><p>“I was born here in 1980, I was living here when they were authorized, I’ve got 40 years of sort of a time lapse to watch,” said Ben Huizenga of the nonprofit Stop Predatory Gambling Illinois. “It has absolutely changed the face of our region, it’s changed what people do with their time.</p><p>“It’s really this kind of invisible parasite on the economy in Illinois.”</p><p>A trade group representing the video gambling industry didn't return calls.</p><p> Pritzker became governor in early 2019, so he didn’t sign the legislation legalizing video gambling.</p><p>But the billionaire Democrat who's toying with a presidential run did sign other legislation that vastly expanded other types of gambling in Illinois, from sports wagering to new casinos.</p><p>Running for a third term in the Nov. 3 general election, Pritzker’s personal investments have included gambling assets over the years, with a past interest in casinos in Elgin, Indiana, the Niagara Falls area and possibly beyond.</p><p>A spokesman for Pritzker’s Republican opponent, Darren Bailey, said local governments “have the ability to opt in” or out of video gambling and “regulate the number of VGTs” and, if elected, he “would keep it that way.”</p><p>Asked whether video gambling has expanded too far, a gaming board spokeswoman said: “Opining or speculating about economic trends in gaming markets and issues involving video gaming saturation are beyond the scope of the IGB’s regulatory and law enforcement mission. The IGB does not conduct market forecasting, provide analysis of economic trends in the Illinois gaming industry, or opine about potential market saturation.”</p><p>Huizenga said, “I’d say we’re actually at the point that we have about as many VGTs as Illinois can absorb.</p><h3>Role sweepstakes machines play</h3><p>While VGTs are regulated, there are similar devices, called sweepstakes machines, that are largely unregulated and located throughout the region, much to the chagrin of the gaming board.</p><p>The agency's "view is that 'sweepstakes' machines are illegal gambling devices that lack supervision by any regulatory body, have no oversight or licensing of any of the establishments, operators or associated individuals," the spokeswoman said. "Sweepstakes machines have no taxation, accounting or operational transparency, and they lack patron protections."</p><p>It's unclear how many of them exist.</p><p>Evanston has sweepstakes machines and is among the communities considering legalizing, regulating and capping them, local officials said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-510000" name="image-510000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/315b67a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0f%2F03%2F9f6dcecf4025b20ed599be34ed4c%2Fpritzkerai-260707-012.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/39cf4ee/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0f%2F03%2F9f6dcecf4025b20ed599be34ed4c%2Fpritzkerai-260707-012.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6e00ec3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0f%2F03%2F9f6dcecf4025b20ed599be34ed4c%2Fpritzkerai-260707-012.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Gov. JB Pritzker, shown earlier this year." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6e00ec3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0f%2F03%2F9f6dcecf4025b20ed599be34ed4c%2Fpritzkerai-260707-012.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d7e1a6d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0f%2F03%2F9f6dcecf4025b20ed599be34ed4c%2Fpritzkerai-260707-012.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6e00ec3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0f%2F03%2F9f6dcecf4025b20ed599be34ed4c%2Fpritzkerai-260707-012.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Gov. JB Pritzker, shown earlier this year.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Even if towns legalize VGTs, the establishments still have to pass muster with the gaming board.</p><p>Joliet has the most VGTs of any municipality in the region, with 561 in more than 100 establishments, gaming board records show. Only Springfield, the state capital, has more statewide, with 835 machines. Cicero, a west suburb, has 446, the second largest total in the metro area, records show.</p><h3>Where Chicago stands on VGTs</h3><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/03/12/video-gambling-battle-chicago-city-council-brandon-johnson-license-committee-rejection" >devices were legalized</a> in Chicago last year against objections from Mayor Brandon Johnson and the developers of the Bally’s Chicago casino, who feared the gambling devices would cannibalize the local market.</p><p>The machines have yet to go live within the city, a City Hall spokesman said.</p><p>Municipalities have been able to allow or ban video gambling from the start, and many of them legalized it because of the expectation of steady revenue. They get a cut of the gaming taxes, as does state government, while the establishments hosting the machines and the companies providing them also share in the income.</p><p>In 2026 alone, through August, Illinois municipalities collectively took in more than $111 million in tax revenues from video gambling, while the state reaped nearly $685 million, records show.</p><p>The net terminal income was more than $2 billion, records show.</p><p>With all that money in play, some municipalities believe their share is too light, such as Robbins, a south suburb that includes many low-income residents and, so far this year, has taken in around $33,000 in gaming tax revenue.</p><p>“There’s some exploitation going on somewhere,” said Darren Bryant, the mayor of Robbins, where there are roughly 4,600 residents and a median household income of around $40,000 a year, nearly half of neighboring Crestwood. “The state should increase the municipality share.”</p><p>Some communities have tried for more revenue by pursuing a “push tax” that puts an additional fee on each button push on a video gambling terminal, but the industry has fought this hard.</p><p>Bryant said: “I’m not the biggest proponent of gaming” largely “because of its impact on residents.”</p><p>He added, “When you don’t need the revenue, you’ve got better options.”</p><p>By contrast, Joliet brought in nearly $2 million last year in video gambling tax revenue, according to gaming board records that show the top grossing location in Illinois in 2025 was a gas station in Forest View. The net terminal income there was more than $4 million, up over 15% compared to the prior year.</p><h3>Some towns start to scale back</h3><p>Some communities believe video gambling has become too saturated within their boundaries and have started to impose limits.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-900000" name="image-900000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" Greg Jackson, chief of staff to Mayor Leon Rockingham Jr., said, “We didn’t want to be known as a little Vegas,” so decided to “reduce the amount of gaming in town” in favor of “other economic development opportunities.”</p><p>“We are going to” continue to “allow gaming, but it’s going to be very controlled,” Jackson said.</p><p>For instance, at least two-third of revenues from any establishment with video gambling now has to come from something besides the devices. So for a restaurant or bar, that probably means food and drink. And officials will no longer allow new licensees to be situated next to others, to avoid clustering.</p><p>“We know we’re going to lose some revenue” initially, but hopefully, it’ll be “made up” down the road, Jackson said. "It's all about quality of life."</p><p>In neighboring Waukegan, there's a casino and more than 300 VGTs, records show.</p><p>Meantime, other communities without video gambling have reversed course or have toyed with the idea.</p><p>Video gambling is banned in Arlington Heights, but local leaders have discussed whether to make it legal. topic to inform any future conversations,” a spokesman said. “At this time, there are no formal proposals being considered by the village board.”</p><p>Downers Grove officials repealed an ordinance allowing gambling after a 2024 referendum.</p><p>La Grange Park village board members "last revisited this issue" in 2023 when they "voted unanimously to uphold Ordinance No. 914, which prohibits video gaming" in the suburb, according to village manager Julia Cedillo.</p><p>In Will County, Frankfort “does not allow it with its corporate limits with the exception of the VFW, which is allowed by state law,” said Frankfort village administrator John Burica, referring to an exemption in the gambling statute that allows veteran and fraternal organizations to have video gambling no matter where they are, so long as meet all other requirements.</p><p>“There are several video gaming machines in establishments located in unincorporated Frankfort, which is under Will County jurisdiction,” Burica said.</p><p>Frankfort is among the last communities in Will that hasn't legalized video gambling.</p><p>Unincorporated areas of all six counties now allow it, including DuPage County where it was legalized for its unincorporated territory in 2019.</p><p>Lake County Board Chairwoman Sandy Hart, a Lake Bluff Democrat, wishes her county government "had greater control over the number of video gambling seats" in her unincorporated areas.</p><p>"As it stands now, if you give them a liquor license you don't have any oversight over video gaming," Hart said.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: White Sox have leaned into strengths with heavy bullpen use, but change is coming
entries.summary: <p>Members of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> regular season starting rotation have lived an alien existence through the postseason.</p><p>“We sit together,” right-hander <b>Erick Fedde</b> told the Sun-Times of life in the bullpen. “We’re talking through our feelings and our nerves. The bullpen's a very different vibe, knowing that we could be called on at any time.”</p><p><b>Davis Martin </b>and <b>Noah Schultz</b> have yet to see a postseason opportunity. But even Sox starters who have gotten a shot have received some unflattering feedback about what matchups the team really thinks they are and aren’t great options to handle.</p><p>“I’ve had a lot of conversations, recently even, with guys,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b>. “It’s OK for you to be upset that I’m taking you out of the game.’ If you were cool with it, then we have a problem. If you didn’t think you could get this guy out, then we have a whole other issue.”</p><p>The Sox have only had a traditional start in four postseason games thus far, and <b>Sean Newcomb</b> opening Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday will make it one in five. <b>Sean Burke</b> is the only Sox starter who has worked in a bulk role, and needed his 5⅓ innings behind an opener in Game 2 to take the team lead in postseason innings from closer <b>Grant Taylor.</b></p><p>It’s a new paradigm from the playoffs pitching heroics most grew up romanticizing, it’s aesthetically displeasing. It’s also, obviously, been effective. The Sox are undefeated in the postseason and have allowed seven earned runs in four games. But rather than trumpet their innovative approach to postseason pitching management, they’re playing the hand they’ve been dealt.</p><p>“I can't say that I wouldn't enjoy having five starters that can provide seven, eight innings,” said general manager <b>Chris Getz</b>. “That's not how we're set up. Was that fully by design? Not necessarily. It was just leaning into our strengths.”</p><p>The Sox bullpen is a strength, their rotation less so. A battle of rotations against the Guardians wouldn’t favor them, and a schedule full of off days has allowed them to avoid it. So, they have.</p><p>At least everyone was warned, as much as was possible.</p><p>“There was talk of some potential for opening, starting, late-leverage, middle bridge guy,” Newcomb said of his preseason understanding of his role. “I guess I'm surprised it maintained being all of it, all year.”</p><h3><b>Change is coming</b></h3><p>However, Wednesday is potentially the start of three games in four days for the Sox. Newcomb is opening Game 3 — reliever <b>Daniel Espino </b>is also opening for the Guardians — but Venable acknowledged the schedule could force the return of more traditional-looking outings from familiar sources of innings.</p><p>“Having off days in between these first three games [of the ALDS], that allowed us to do some things and that is not going to be the case anymore,” Venable said. “We're going to see some arms [in Game 3] potentially that we haven't seen yet in this series or even in the playoffs.”</p><h3><b>Mune loves Will</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Venable’s substantive conversations with his All-Star first baseman <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> still occur through interpreter <b>Kenzo Yagi</b>, yet the Japanese slugger still praises him for his communication skills.</p><p>“I just love him as a person, and I'm really happy that he's my manager,” Murakami said via interpreter. “That's pretty much what I feel about Will.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/06/chicago-white-sox-rivals-cleveland-guardians-will-venable-stephen-vogt-sam-antonacci-sean-newcomb-jordan-hicks-brewers-tigers-twins-bulls-cavaliers" >White Sox need a rival, and Guardians fit the bill — they just have to dislike each other</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Former Itasca, West Chicago police officers charged with misusing Flock cameras
entries.summary: <p>A former Itasca police officer and an ex-West Chicago police officer are both facing felony charges for allegedly making “unauthorized forbidden” searches of Flock license plate reader databases, according to the DuPage County state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>Marisa Ciccola, 30, who previously was an Itasca police officer, and former West Chicago officer Gerardo Solis, were charged by a grand jury in September and turned themselves in Tuesday before being released on bond, the office said.</p><p>Ciccola faces 13 counts of official misconduct and eight counts of computer tampering, while Solis was charged with official misconduct and a single count of computer tampering. They both are set to appear in court again Nov. 16.</p><p>Between June 2025 and May 2026, Ciccola is alleged to have made unauthorized searches while Solis was accused of doing so at least once between Dec. 18, 2024, and Jan. 15, 2025, according to prosecutors. Both of their respective former police agencies said they will cooperate with investigators.</p><p>The two are the latest in an ongoing epidemic of alleged police misuse of the mass surveillance system.</p><p>Early last month, West Chicago announced it was reviewing its use of Flock cameras after officials <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/01/illinois-cities-halt-flock-use-suspend-officers-and-review-policy-amid-alleged-improper-use" target="_blank" ><u>announced an investigation</u></a> of Solis. The Channahon Police Department in Will County said it was conducting a similar review after an investigation found that its officers may have also made unauthorized searches. The accused officers were placed on leave.</p><p>Those actions came at the same time that southwest suburban Homer Glen announced that it was suspending the use of Flock cameras within its borders “pending final determination of the investigation and review of the Sheriff’s ALPR protocol” after a Will County sheriff’s deputy was placed on administrative leave amid allegations he misused the technology.</p><p>In recent months, a part-time Prairie Grove cop, who was also serving as the chief of police for Holiday Hills, was accused of abusing the system to stalk people he knew, with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/former-holiday-hills-police-chief-charged-with-making-nearly-300-unauthorized-searches-court-records" target="_blank" ><u>nearly 250 unauthorized searches of their license plate movements</u></a>. That officer faces multiple felony charges of official misconduct.</p><p>In August, Frank McGrath, a former Kenosha County, Wisconsin, sheriff’s deputy, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/27/flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-chicago-suburb" target="_blank" ><u>hit with felony charges</u></a> after an audit revealed he’d used Flock to spy on a co-worker, according to the agency.</p><p>DuPage County State’s Attorney Robert Berlin said despite the charges against Ciccola, Solis and others, license plate reader cameras are a “crucial component of law enforcement” that had led to arrests.</p><p>“Misuse of this technology, however, must carry consequences, and anyone who breaches the public trust in such a manner will be held accountable,” Berlin said in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.dupagecounty.gov/state_s_attorney/former_itasca_and_west_chicago_police_officers_charged_1770.php" target="_blank" ><u>statement</u></a>.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/01/illinois-cities-halt-flock-use-suspend-officers-and-review-policy-amid-alleged-improper-use" >Illinois suburbs halt Flock use, suspend officers and review policy amid alleged improper use</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/17/five-public-universities-in-illinois-use-controversial-flock-cameras-to-surveil-campus" >5 public universities in Illinois use Flock surveillance cameras on campus, records show</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/27/flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-chicago-suburb" >Flock license plate readers turn Chicago suburbs into ground zero for bitter fight over surveillance</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Pilsen llora la muerte de influencer Paola Zamora Rojas tras su batalla de salud mental
entries.summary: <p>La familia de Paola Judith Zamora Rojas se reunió en su departamento en Pilsen, como lo ha hecho muchas noches desde su muerte.</p><p>Las sillas estaban frente a un altar decorado con fotografías de la madre de 32 años de edad. Era el viernes pasado, la cuarta noche de una novena católica de nueve días.</p><p>Las veladoras cerca del altar representaban a San Judas. La hermana mayor de Zamora Rojas, Yahaira Gutiérrez, dijo que su madre, Sandra Zamora, le rezó al santo cuando Zamora Rojas dejó de respirar durante una experiencia cercana a la muerte cuando ella era bebé.</p><p>La familia cree que su sobrevivencia fue "una especie de milagro", dijo Yahaira Gutiérrez. Sandra Zamora le puso a su hija el segundo nombre Judith en honor al santo.</p><p>Más de tres décadas después, las veladoras de San Judas siguen encendidas mientras la familia vuelve a rezar por ella.</p><p>Zamora Rojas murió por suicidio el 17 de septiembre, después de lo que amigos y familiares describieron como una larga batalla contra una enfermedad de salud mental.</p><p>El ojo que tenía Zamora Rojas para la moda le había ganado decenas de miles de seguidores en las redes sociales. Alrededor había rastros de la vida que había vivido: discos de segunda mano, muebles vintage y hallazgos usados.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-credit"><p>Octavio Jones/Para el Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>También asistió Diana Galicia Corona, cuyo hijo, Gabriel Cisneros, había sido el prometido de Zamora Rojas.</p><p>Zamora Rojas tenía tres meses de embarazo de su hija, Olivia, cuando Cisneros, de 22 años, murió por una sobredosis accidental de heroína el Día de las Madres de 2016. Después de eso, Zamora Rojas siguió llamando a Galicia Corona su suegra. Ella dijo que consideraba a Zamora Rojas su nuera.</p><p>Una semana antes de la muerte de Cisneros, Galicia Corona recuerda que salió de un restaurante en Pilsen con la joven pareja cuando empezó a sonar música. Su hijo tomó la mano de Zamora Rojas, la hizo girar y bailó con ella en la acera.</p><p>"Lo que Gabriel y Paola tenían era una historia de amor que nunca debió terminar", dijo Galicia Corona.</p><p>La familia dijo que Zamora Rojas nunca dejó de llorar su muerte. Galicia Corona vio que ese dolor reaparecía en su cumpleaños, en las fiestas y en el aniversario de la muerte de su hijo.</p><p>El duelo y la depresión eran solo parte de una vida que su familia describió como extraordinariamente plena.</p><p>Zamora Rojas criaba a su hija que adoraba, revendía ropa por internet, asistía a conciertos y recibía en su casa a músicos de gira.</p><p>Les mostraba Chicago a nuevos amigos y apoyaba a artistas y negocios de Pilsen, dijo su familia.</p><p>Y muchas veces era la persona a la que otros acudían cuando estaban pasando por un mal momento.</p><div entries.title: City replaces homemade benches in Ukrainian Village with ADA-compliant seating
entries.summary: <p>A neighborhood group’s effort to make public transit more accessible for riders paid off after city officials installed benches at two CTA bus stops in Ukrainian Village.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/14/cta-bus-stop-bench-ukrainian-village" target="_blank" >Last month</a>, the Northwest Neighborhood Alliance installed two homemade benches — one at Damen Avenue and Thomas Street and another at Division Street and Oakley Boulevard — to provide a place for residents who rely on public transit to sit while waiting for their bus.</p><p>The two benches, painted in the colors of the Ukrainian flag, caught the attention and city officials, who on Monday replaced them with ADA-compliant benches.</p><p>“This was the best outcome that we could have hoped for,” said Sam Kovnar, 25, founder of the local group.</p><p>Kovnar said the benches provided more than just a place to sit, offering relief for riders with mobility issues, as well as children and older adults.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-400000" In September, the Northwest Neighborhood Alliance installed two homemade benches — one here and one at Damen Avenue — to provide a place for residents who rely on public transit to sit while waiting for their bus.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Chicago Transit Authority has almost 11,000 bus stops in Chicago, but many don’t have benches as part of a city push to deter loitering.</p><p>A spokesperson for the Chicago Department of Transportation said it “works with ward offices to identify locations for benches, which can be advertising benches or other benches installed using aldermanic menu funds.”</p><p>Ald. entries.title: White Sox seemingly try to make Guardians sad, sleepy with workout music playlist
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> didn't exactly play workout music during the Guardians' workout Tuesday at Rate Field.</p><p>Seemingly trying to play mind games with their playoff opponent, Sox' crack music staff played sad, slow and sleepy tunes as the Guardians prepared for Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday (3 p.m., TBS, truTV, 1000-AM).</p><p>The playlist began, appropriately, with Boyz II Men's "End Of The Road." The Guardians trail the best-of-five series 2-0. It continued with The Sundays' "Here’s Where the Story Ends," Daniel Powter's "Bad Day" and R.E.M.'s "Everybody Hurts."</p><p>The playlist shifted to the soothing sounds of Savage Garden's "Truly Madly Deeply," Paula Cole's "I Don't Want to Wait" and the Cranberries' "Linger." The songs then were accompanied by Sox season highlights on the center-field video board. It was practically sensory overload for the poor Guardians.</p><p>The Sox also played the Crash Test Dummies' "Mmm Mmm Mmm Mmm," Eric Clapton's "Wonderful Tonight," Sixpence None the Richer's "Kiss Me" and Snow Patrol's "Chasing Cars."</p><p>It wasn't the first time the Sox tried messing with a Cleveland team. In April 2002, the stadium music director greeted Cleveland pitcher Chuck Finley with Whitesnake's "Here I Go Again," a reference to Finley's divorce from actress Tawny Kitaen, who starred in the rock group's videos. The Sox fired the director the next day.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/06/chicago-white-sox-rivals-cleveland-guardians-will-venable-stephen-vogt-sam-antonacci-sean-newcomb-jordan-hicks-brewers-tigers-twins-bulls-cavaliers" >White Sox need a rival, and Guardians fit the bill — they just have to dislike each other</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Amazon taking over long-vacant West Town warehouse for same-day deliveries
entries.summary: <p>Amazon purchased Chicago’s first vertical logistics building last week to use as a same-day delivery center.</p><p>The Seattle-based e-commerce giant purchased the two-story building at 1237 W. Division St. for $195 million, Crain's Chicago Business first reported.</p><p>“Doing this allows us to effectively … make a delivery in a matter of a couple of hours instead of a couple of days and really shortens that distance that any vehicle — whether it be truck, van, or car — needs to travel to reach customers,” said Kyle DeGiulio, Amazon’s senior manager of economic development policy for the Midwest. “We’re really excited to expand our footprint in Chicago.”</p><p>Amazon plans to start operations in late 2027 or early 2028. The West Town property, near Goose Island, will be a “sub-same day fulfillment center” combining warehousing and delivery functions, DeGiulio said. </p><p>Rather than using fleet vehicles, like Amazon’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/7/21/23272625/amazon-electric-delivery-fleet-rivian-climate-streets-transportation" >electric Rivian vans</a>, deliveries will be made by Amazon Flex drivers — workers who use their own vehicles, akin to DoorDash or Uber drivers.</p><p>The facility will create 200 jobs, from fulfillment to managerial roles, with an average hourly wage near $24, according to DeGiulio. Amazon employees in Chicago will be offered the opportunity to transfer to the Division Street site.</p><p>The warehouse will be Amazon’s second same-day delivery center in Chicago. It has a similar center in West Humboldt Park that opened in 2023, despite the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2024/11/27/amazon-overcomes-critics-west-humboldt-park-fulfillment-center-community-roots" >ire of neighbors</a>.</p><p>DeGiulio said the new location will meet customers' growing appetite for same-day deliveries, particularly for groceries and pharmaceuticals, that it's seeing in Chicago and all of its markets. </p><p>“There's a lot of things that people want from Amazon very, very quickly that exist in buildings that are farther away and take a little bit of time,” he said. “Now, understanding customer behavior a little bit, the types of items that people want quickly, a site like this just gives us a better opportunity to serve them and also serves in an area where we feel that the surrounding infrastructure supports that operation, rather than trying to just drop this somewhere where it doesn't necessarily fit.”</p><p>DeGiulio said Amazon has eyed the Goose Island area for a while but was waiting for the right opportunity. The Division Street site is “highly visible” and desirable for its quick highway access. It's also near thoroughfares like Elston Avenue, allowing drivers to get across the city faster.</p><p>He acknowledged the area's traffic congestion, but said the city's infrastructure investments — like replacing the two Division Street bridges — made the company bullish on the location.</p><p>Logistics Property Co. broke ground on the roughly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/24/23415668/west-town-multistory-warehouse-logistics-property" >590,000-square-foot warehouse</a> in 2022. At the time, the property was the first multistory warehouse in Chicago, boasting truck docks on both floors and more than 1,000 parking spaces. But the building has remained vacant since its 2024 completion. Logistics Property tapped real estate firm JLL to help market the property.</p><p>Logistics Property declined to comment.</p><p>A marketing brochure from JLL and developer Logistics Property said the building is five minutes away from the Loop and 15 minutes from O’Hare Airport. It also boasted an estimated $2 billion in e-commerce sales within a 5-mile radius.</p><p>Amazon owns multilevel warehouses across the U.S. and internationally, DeGiulio said. But this property is unique for its exterior, featuring murals and a colorful parking ramp visible from the Kennedy Expressway.</p><p>“It's almost like this building was built for us to use,” he said.</p>

entries.title: White Sox need a rival, and Guardians fit the bill — they just have to dislike each other
entries.summary: <p>White Sox manager Will Venable has immense respect for his Guardians counterpart, Stephen Vogt. Venable thinks Vogt is among the best managers in baseball because of his strategizing and the way players play for him.</p><p>“He is as good as they get,” Venable said. “But also, because of that, you want to beat him, too.”</p><p>That’s the extent of the trash-talking between the teams. They have the cleanest trash in the neighborhood.</p><p>Such is the nature of the Guardians-<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> rivalry. Despite a hotly contested 13-game season series that saw the teams’ battle for the Central crown go down to the final weekend, plus the first two postseason meetings in their shared history, there is no animosity whatsoever.</p><p>“What’s special about this rivalry is that there's a lot of respect on both sides,” Venable said.</p><p>Special doesn’t come to mind. Lackluster, muted and uninspired do.</p><p>Yes, the games have been great. But where’s the dislike? Where’s the resentment? Where are the brushbacks, the chirps, the staredowns?</p><p>What happened to baseball rivalries?</p><p>Sox reliever Jordan Hicks played in one of baseball’s best rivalries, Cardinals-Cubs, in his first five seasons, starting in 2018.</p><p>“That one felt real when I was a rookie,” Hicks said. “Maybe it’s a young thing.”</p><p>As if to say, it was fun when I was a kid; then I grew up.</p><p>“Since I’ve been in the league, the nastiness has been very small, from what I’ve seen,” said Sox left-hander Sean Newcomb, who came up with the Braves in 2017. “It’s definitely there. I’d say everyone kind of keeps it within themselves.”</p><p>Well, let it out, guys!</p><p>The Sox have had blood feuds before. In the early days of the American League Central, the Sox and Brewers had a few memorable dust-ups, including one with managers Terry Bevington and Phil Garner going at it.</p><p>The Sox-Tigers brawl-game in 2000 is legendary. The Sox and Twins didn’t get along in the 2000s, so much so that Torii Hunter once bowled over catcher Jamie Burke, a cheap shot that still lives in infamy.</p><p>But none of those rivalries extended to the postseason. This could be the first of many playoff series between the Sox and Guardians. At some point, familiarity breeds contempt, right?</p><p>“You typically see these guys the most, so you kind of make a little conversation,” Guardians right fielder Chase DeLauter said.</p><p>That’s so sweet. Are they planning Tupperware parties, too?</p><p>Where’s Albert Belle when you need him?</p><p>I needed a kindred spirit in competitive chippiness, someone who isn’t afraid to spark a fire, someone who likes chicken wings.</p><p>I approached Sam Antonacci, who would have two minor penalties for elbowing if baseball included such infractions. Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras and Pirates second baseman Brandon Lowe have been recipients of Antonacci’s left elbow this season, the latter leading to the benches clearing.</p><p>In his rookie year with the Sox, Antonacci hasn’t felt a rivalry with anyone, saying such animosity seems reserved for fans. But he also said he’d like to see less chatter among combatants.</p><p>“Obviously, mutual respect before the game and after the game,” he said, “but across the white lines, you see guys chatting it up when they get to second base or third base, whereas back in the day, it feels like you weren’t talking to anybody. Not that it’s a bad thing, but it’s a change.”</p><p>A change for the worse. You can demonstrate sportsmanship without hugs and butt taps with the opposition. It’s OK to want to pulverize an opponent. No, this isn’t football or hockey — I love hockey; can you tell? — but feel free to push the envelope, guys, if only for fans’ entertainment.</p><p>Guardians-Sox could be a thing. We need a Chicago-Cleveland rivalry. Bears-Browns is nothing, and Bulls-Cavaliers has been dormant for a decade. Do the Sox harbor any resentment at all toward the team that stole the division crown from them?</p><p>“I feel like there’s no bad blood,” Hicks said. “We just want to beat them.”</p><p>That’s certainly mature and professional — not to mention boring.</p><p>“I guess it’s got to be set off by something,” Newcomb said. “I don’t think we’re going to search for it.”</p><p>Maybe this playoff series will be that spark, whether the Sox finish the sweep Wednesday or the Guardians rally. If the Sox are going to be good in the foreseeable future, games will mean more and rivalries figure to follow.</p><p>But there’s a ready-made one right in front of us. It just needs the fuel to ignite.</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/06/chicago-white-sox-cleveland-guardians-workout-music-playlist-alds-mlb-playoff-postseason" >White Sox seemingly try to make Guardians sad, sleepy with workout music playlist</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
